places.notes: The cafe was born from a mother's personal struggle: the owner's daughter had severe egg allergies and childhood asthma, and the family constantly found it hard to share meals while traveling because everyday foods like bread, cake and ice cream contained eggs. Watching her daugh
places.chef: Hirai Kaori (平井薫) · owner, operator · Naramachi, Nara · The cafe was born from a mother's personal struggle: the owner's daughter had severe egg allergies and childhood asthma, and the family constantly found it hard to share meals while traveling because everyday foods like bread, cake and ice cream contained eggs. Watching her daughter be handed fruit or sorbet while everyone else enjoyed ice cream inspired her to build a place where that exclusion would never happen. Surveys also showed overseas visitors to Nara felt there were too few vegetarian-friendly restaurants. After originally operating in the Mochiidono shopping arcade, the cafe relocated and reopened on July 1, 2023 in a spacious traditional wooden machiya in Higashishiodo-cho. · Vegan, delicious and healthy — a table where anyone can eat the same food together whether or not they are vegan, vegetarian or have a food allergy, so no one is left out. · Fully vegan, gluten-free and nut-free fare: vegan ice cream, gluten-free muffins, parfaits, lunch sets, an omakase course and takeout bento, with seasonal limited dishes. Flavor is built from kombu, shiitake and vegetable stock and fermented seasonings.
places.gfd: Fully dedicated gluten-free kitchen. Every item on the menu is completely vegan, gluten-free and nut-free, and the kitchen deliberately avoids wheat, soba (buckwheat) and peanuts entirely. Umami is built from kombu, shiitake and vegetable stock rather than wheat-based seasonings. Because no wheat enters the kitchen at all, this is one of the rare genuinely celiac-friendly options in central Nara; diners with severe restrictions are still asked to contact the shop in advance.
places.vgd: 100% plant-based. Every dish, dessert and drink is fully vegan with no animal products, eggs or dairy. Offerings include vegan ice cream, gluten-free muffins, parfaits, lunch sets and an omakase course, with seasonal limited-time dishes.
places.hours: 12:00-17:00; closed Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. Hours may change — confirm before visiting.

places.chef: owner-operated · Nara (Takahata-cho) · A small, owner-run vegan cafe tucked into a quiet lane in the Takahata district on the eastern edge of Naramachi, near the historic Nara Hotel and within reach of Kasuga Taisha. Everything is made by hand in-house, drawing on the owners' background working at a natural-foods store. · 100% vegan whole-foods cooking that is additive-free and organic wherever possible: brown rice, 100% whole-grain bread, largely organic vegetables and organic seasonings, favoring lively, unprocessed ingredients. No animal products of any kind (including gelatin and honey). The owners care deeply about animal welfare and keep the cafe a sincerely vegan space. · Plant-based comfort food and sweets: a juicy soy-meat karaage that surprises diners with how meat-like it tastes, a vegan hamburg plate and burgers, soy-based nuggets, an organic legume-and-vegetable curry, egg-style sandwiches, a shoyu ramen, enzyme/brown-rice plate lunches, and dairy-free cakes, tarts and ohagi.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free and not celiac-safe. While rice dishes use natural-farming brown rice, the kitchen makes its own bread, cakes and tarts from 100% whole-grain wheat flour, and the menu features soy-meat dishes (karaage, nuggets, burgers) and a shoyu (wheat-based soy sauce) ramen. Wheat is used throughout the bakery and savory menu and there is no dedicated gluten-free preparation, so this is not suitable for someone requiring strict gluten avoidance. Ask staff directly if pursuing any GF option.
places.vgd: Fully vegan (100% plant-based, whole-foods style). No animal products at all — no meat, fish, dairy, egg, gelatin or honey — and no white/refined sugar. Bread is made with organic whole-grain flour and natural yeast, rice is natural-farming brown rice, vegetables are largely pesticide-free, seasonings are traditionally-made organic, and coffee is self-roasted organic Colombian. places.chef: 三浦雅之 (Masayuki Miura) — owner/representative & farmer; 新子大輔 (Atarashi Daisuke) — chef and manager · owner, chef, farmer · Nara City — Naramachi historic district, with its own pesticide-free farm in the nearby Gokaya (former Gokaya Village) hills · Awa occupies a townhouse in the narrow lanes of Naramachi that has stood for around 140 years and was carefully renovated to keep its old machiya character, with counter seats and tatami rooms looking onto an interior garden over two floors. It is the flagship dining room of a Nara food-culture project based in the Gokaya (former Gokaya Village) area of Nara City, which pairs restaurant work with farming and research into the region's heritage crops. · The team treats small-scale heirloom varieties as 'family vegetables' (家族野菜), grown with care for personal use and sharing with neighbors rather than mass production. places.chef: 老舗（しにせ）柿の葉寿司店, 郷土料理店, 手作り体験提供 · Yoshino, Nara Prefecture (奈良県吉野・上市村) · Hiraso traces its founding to 1861 (Bunkyū 1), when Hirai Sōhachi opened a shop dealing in sushi, river fish, and dried goods in Kami-Ichimura, Yoshino, deep in Nara's mountains. The house name 平宗 fuses the founder's surname Hirai (平) with a character from his given name Sōhachi (宗). The Nara branch opened in 1968 (Shōwa 43) in the Naramachi district beside Sarusawa Pond, where guests dine within earshot of Kōfuku-ji temple's bell. · The house describes its work as carrying on the dedication of its predecessors and the care demanded when preparing food fit even for imperial offering — a craftsman's reverence applied to a humble regional dish. · Kaki-no-ha-zushi (persimmon-leaf sushi) wrapping vinegared rice and salted fish such as mackerel and salmon in aromatic persimmon leaves, served alongside Nara local fare like cha-gayu (tea rice porridge), Miwa somen / nyūmen, and seasonal set meals.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. Signature kaki-no-ha sushi is vinegared rice that is fine in itself, but the menu centers on wheat-heavy dishes (にゅうめん/三輪素麺 somen, tempura) and soy sauce, and fish/dashi-based seasonings are used throughout. No dedicated gluten-free preparation or celiac handling is documented.
places.vgd: Not a vegan destination. The signature kaki-no-ha sushi is topped with fish (mackerel/saba, salmon), and set meals include sashimi (お造り), fish, and dashi/煮麺 broths that are typically fish-based. Items like 胡麻豆腐 (sesame tofu) and 茶粥 (tea rice porridge) may be plant-based but are not served as a verified vegan menu, and no vegan accommodation is documented.

The owner, Ueshima, came across the long-abandoned house and—after carefully cleaning and restoring it, keeping latticed win
places.chef: Ueshima · owner, café founder · Naramachi, Nara City · Kanakana is a café set inside a roughly century-old Nara townhouse (machiya) in the historic Naramachi district, near the former grounds of Gangoji Temple. The owner, Ueshima, came across the long-abandoned house and—after carefully cleaning and restoring it, keeping latticed windows, exposed wooden columns and the remains of an old hearth—realized a dream she had held since her student days to open her own café. It is widely regarded as one of the pioneering townhouse cafés that sparked the Naramachi café boom, and even on weekday mornings a line often forms before opening. · The kitchen works to a simple idea of 'warmth in cooking'—warm dishes are served hot and cold dishes cold—and the room is furnished with vintage pieces and folk art to create a nostalgic, welcoming space; the coffee has long been sourced from the same Gifu roaster (milou) specifically to keep the experience consistent for regulars. · The signature dish is the all-day 'Kanakana-gohan' set: a daily-changing home-style spread of a main (such as pan-fried cod in tomato sauce or a pork-and-tomato hotpot) with several small vegetable, tofu and konnyaku side di…
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly and not suitable for celiacs. The daily set meal and dishes rely on standard Japanese seasonings (soy sauce, miso) and the café also serves homemade cakes, cheesecake and baked pudding. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no celiac accommodation is documented.
places.vgd: Not a vegetarian or vegan destination. The signature daily カナカナごはん is a home-style Japanese set built around fish and meat (e.g., pan-fried cod, pork-and-tomato hotpot) plus miso soup that typically uses fish dashi, so it is not vegan by default. There is no published vegan/vegetarian menu; a plant-eater would have to ask in person about that day's dishes, and options cannot be guaranteed.

places.chef: owner-grower · Nara (Funahashicho) · Cafe Koyomi sits on the old-fashioned Funahashi shopping street (船橋商店街) just east of Kintetsu Nara Station, in a calm space lined with Japanese paper (washi) and cypress (hinoki) that the owner likens to a cozy living room. The owner grows much of the produce and rice herself, then cooks lunch to match the season. · The name KOYOMI means 'calendar/almanac': just as the seasons turn (季節に移ろい暦があるように), the owner believes food has its own season, and prepares each dish slowly and 'ひとつひとつ丁寧に' (with careful attention to every element) using vegetables grown over time. · The signature lunch is the seasonal 馳走膳 (chisō-zen) set and the 'Koyomi bowl', built around home-grown vegetables, beans and pot-cooked rice with a homemade-miso soup. Sweets are vegan, gluten-free cakes and weekly-changing treats made from the owner's own rice flour, with no dairy, egg, or white sugar; coffee is ground to order and pressed in a French press.

places.chef: owner-operator · Pleased To Meet Me — known affectionately as Puritomi — is a tiny, owner-run kissa in the quiet Kitamachi side of central Nara (Hōren-chō), about a ten-minute walk north of Kintetsu Nara Station. Opened on 1 March 2017, it blurs the line between café, bar and record shop: the room carries a nostalgic Showa-era mood, with vintage collectibles on the shelves and analog vinyl for sale alongside the food and drinks. · Music and hospitality are part of the experience as much as the food; the owner works largely solo and keeps the place personal and unhurried. · The house signature is the falafel — chickpea fritters fried with spices, Middle Eastern style — served either as a pita sandwich or as a plate, layered with deep-fried eggplant, tomato and lettuce for a dish of contrasting textures and no meat. On weekends the owner makes a vegetable curry (which often sells out), and the bar side pours craft beer, homemade ginger ale and fruit juices.

Celiac and gluten-sensitive diners must ask in person before ordering; nothing here is confirmed safe.

On a trip to Nara she tasted Miwa sōmen from Sakurai and was so struck by how dif
places.chef: Takeda Kaori · owner, chef · Kantō / Kanagawa Prefecture · Owner Takeda Kaori grew up in the Kantō region (Kanagawa) and first worked as a company employee while earning a cooking license, then spent about two years training at a French restaurant in Osaka. On a trip to Nara she tasted Miwa sōmen from Sakurai and was so struck by how different it was from any sōmen she'd had that she resolved to move to Nara and open a shop devoted to it. · She builds the broth on the French fish-stock technique fumet de poisson — simmered from sea-bream bones — and pairs it with sōmen because, as she puts it, the beauty of sōmen is its simplicity: it is the finest of noodles and goes wonderfully with a good dashi. · The signature is tai-dashi sōmen (about ¥1,000): hand-pulled Miwa sōmen from a Sakurai maker served warm in a clear sea-bream broth, finished with a secret salt sauce and aromatics like ginger-garlic oil and rosemary. A French-and-Italian twist, tai-dashi tomato sōmen, uses whole-wheat noodles, and seasonal versions include cream and chicken keema styles, often served as a tasting set with small appetizers, dessert and a drink.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. Sōmen and nyūmen are wheat-flour noodles, and one signature dish (tai-dashi tomato sōmen) is made on whole-wheat noodles. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no celiac accommodation. Unsafe for celiac and gluten-avoidant diners.
places.vgd: Not vegan. The kitchen is built around a sea-bream (tai) fish broth — the owner adapted the French fish-stock technique fumet de poisson made from simmered fish bones — so the core dishes are fish-based. No documented vegan menu or plant-based dashi option.

places.notes: Shunsai Hiyori sits at the entrance to Naramachi, on the first floor of the Uzuraiya Club building next to the World Heritage temple Gangoji, with a Nara rakugo storytelling hall upstairs. From a modest storefront it opens into a surprisingly spacious dining room of tables, count
places.chef: vegetable-focused Japanese restaurant, kaiseki dining · Naramachi, central Nara · Shunsai Hiyori sits at the entrance to Naramachi, on the first floor of the Uzuraiya Club building (鶉屋倶楽部) near the World Heritage temple Gangoji, with the Nara rakugo storytelling hall (奈良町落語館) on the second floor. places.chef: sushi shop, tea house / eat-in, souvenir shop · Gojo, Nara Prefecture · Kakinoha Sushi Honpo Tanaka traces its roots to the late Meiji era in Gojo, Nara. The founder, Tanaka Tokumatsu, was a master carpenter whose wife Yoshi cooked for his many craftsmen; the family later ran a diner in the shopping street by Gojo Station, where the persimmon-leaf sushi they made only in summer became the origin of the company's product. Tokumatsu's grandson Shuji took over, and the kakinoha-zushi made by his wife Taka grew into a local specialty that drew customers from Osaka and Kobe. Deciding to make it the family's main trade, Shuji formally established the company in 1973. This Nara flagship sits at the entrance of the Higashimuki shopping street just outside Kintetsu Nara Station. · Operating under the concept of 'tradition and innovation' (伝統と革新), the company aims not only to preserve the regional dish of kakinoha-zushi but to keep adding something new, researching persimmon-leaf salting techniques and expanding nationwide shipping. · Kakinoha-zushi (persimmon-leaf sushi) wrapped in salted persimmon leaves, with mackerel (saba), salmon, sea bream, conger eel and red tuna; eat-in sets pairin…
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. Celiac travelers should treat this as unsafe.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Sakura is a kuzu sweets shop (甘味処) opened by a kimono merchant (呉服店) whose business dates to the Meiji era, set in the historic Naramachi district near Kintetsu Nara Station.
places.chef: family-run confectionery · Naramachi, Nara — Takamikadomachi · Sakura is a kuzu sweets shop (甘味処) opened by a kimono merchant (呉服店) whose business dates to the Meiji era, set in the historic Naramachi district near Kintetsu Nara Station. · Because true hon-kuzu turns cloudy and changes flavor as time passes, every order is prepared fresh by hand only after the customer orders, preserving the clarity and delicate texture of the arrowroot. · Desserts made from 100% rare Yoshino hon-kuzu (true Yoshino arrowroot): kuzukiri (translucent arrowroot noodles) and kuzumochi (arrowroot mochi), served plain or with matcha and kuromitsu syrup.
places.gfd: The signature kuzukiri and kuzumochi are made from 100% Yoshino hon-kuzu (arrowroot starch), which is naturally gluten-free. However, this is a traditional sweets shop with no documented allergen handling, and some kuzu confections elsewhere are blended with wheat or served with sweetened soy/kinako that may carry gluten. There is no information confirming dedicated equipment or cross-contamination controls, so a celiac diner must ask directly about ingredients and preparation before ordering.
places.vgd: The core kuzukiri and kuzumochi are plant-based (arrowroot starch served with kuromitsu black-sugar syrup and/or matcha), which can be vegan. But honey, kinako, or dairy/cream may appear in some seasonal items and accompaniments, and ingredients are not documented for vegans. Confirm syrups and toppings before ordering.
places.hours: 10:00–17:00; closed Wednesdays and Thursdays (open on holidays)

places.chef: tofu maker, restaurant · Tenri, Nara (Kondo Tofu Shop) · Naramachi Tofu-an Kondo is the sit-down restaurant of Kondo Tofu Shop, a tofu maker based in Tenri, who opened this place to let visitors taste their tofu cooked many ways. It occupies a roughly 180-year-old townhouse (at Nishi-Shinya-cho) in the old merchant quarter of Naramachi that is registered as a Tangible Cultural Property, complete with an interior courtyard garden. · Cherishing the natural flavor of the ingredient: tofu is made only from carefully selected 100% domestic soybeans (such as Kyushu Fukuyutaka and Hokuriku Enrei) set with mineral-rich Izu Oshima sea nigari, to bring out a deep, mellow bean taste. · Tofu set meals built around yudofu (hot tofu in a soy-milk style broth), oboro tofu eaten with sea salt, dashi soy sauce or yuzu pepper, fresh yuba and oboro sashimi, agedashi tofu, dengaku, okara and hirousu, often finished with a sweet.
places.gfd: Not a gluten-free destination. No gluten-free menu or celiac-safe protocol is documented. A celiac traveler would need to ask in detail and should not assume safety.
places.vgd: Tofu-focused and plant-forward (yudofu, oboro tofu, fresh yuba, okara, ganmodoki), so there is genuine vegan potential, but it is not a vegan restaurant. Set meals are built around dashi and soy sauce that are commonly fish/bonito-based, and items like hirousu/ganmodoki and clear soup may contain fish dashi. No documented vegan menu; a vegan diner must confirm the dashi and broth ingredients befo…

The name 荷茶屋 ("carried teahouse") recalls the old custom of vendors who carried tea and refresh
places.chef: teahouse / 甘味処 on the Kasuga Taisha approach · On the grounds of Kasuga Taisha, 奈良公園, central Nara. · Kasuga Ninaijaya is a garden teahouse set right along the wooded approach to Kasuga Taisha, near the Manyo Botanical Garden, where pilgrims and park visitors have long stopped to rest. The name 荷茶屋 ("carried teahouse") recalls the old custom of vendors who carried tea and refreshments to shrine-goers, and the shop carries that tradition into a quiet spot among the seasonal flowering trees of the Kasuga forest. · A seasonal, place-rooted menu that lets diners taste the changing year — vegetables and dishes rotate month by month, served in a garden where the forest seasons are part of the meal. · The signature dish is 万葉粥 (manyo porridge), a gentle rice porridge simmered in Hokkaido kombu dashi and Nara white miso with monthly-changing seasonal vegetables inspired by the Man'yoshu poetry anthology, made with Hinohikari rice. It anchors the 大和名物膳 set (porridge, two pieces of saba persimmon-leaf sushi, seasonal kuzumochi, a side and pickles), and in summer the shop serves traditional Kasuga 春日素麺 eaten the old way with umeboshi and mustard. Sweets include Yoshino-kuzu kuzumochi, matcha…
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. Core offerings contain wheat: the summer 春日素麺 (somen) is wheat noodles, the kuzumochi and other cakes contain wheat, and the persimmon-leaf sushi involves soy. White miso and the seasoning are typical wheat-containing Japanese condiments. There is no gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and a celiac visitor cannot eat safely here. Even the rice porridge risks cross-contact in a shared kitchen serving noodles and cakes.
places.vgd: The signature 万葉粥 (manyo porridge) is made with Hokkaido kombu dashi and Nara white miso — no fish dashi — so it can be a plant-based option, and there are sweets like Yoshino kuzumochi and matcha. However this is not a vegan kitchen: the popular set meals include saba (mackerel) persimmon-leaf sushi, white miso may not be confirmed dashi-free in every preparation, and there is no formal vegan me…

places.chef: Okada · owner, ice craftsman · Nara · Houseki-bako opened in March 2015 inside the Mochiidono Yume CUBE, helping to launch Nara's now-famous kakigori (shaved ice) boom. Demand grew so intense that the original shop had to restrict entry, and in March 2018 it relocated to a roomier space further along the same Mochiidono shopping arcade. · The owner, Okada-san, shaves the ice for every order himself, believing that the hand doing the shaving directly affects the texture of the finished ice. · Espuma kakigori: finely shaved ice crowned with airy foam ("espuma") made from milk or yogurt, layered with seasonal fruit syrups and toppings. The contrast between the delicate ice and the creamy foam is the shop's signature.
places.gfd: A kakigori (shaved ice) specialist. Plain shaved ice with fruit syrups can be naturally gluten-free, but the signature dishes use milk/yogurt espuma and varied seasonal syrups/toppings, and there is no documented gluten-free protocol or allergen labeling. Anyone with celiac disease should ask about each component before ordering, as ingredients change seasonally and cross-contact in a small kitchen cannot be ruled out.
places.vgd: The signature creations are built on dairy: milk espuma and yogurt espuma are central to the menu, so the headline dishes are not vegan. A simple fruit-syrup shaved ice without the dairy foam might be possible, but there is no documented vegan option. Ask staff whether a dairy-free version can be made.
places.hours: 10:00-13:00, 14:00-16:50 (Mon, Tue, Wed, Fri); 10:00-13:00, 14:00-17:20 (Sat, Sun); closed Thursdays. Web reservation only, opening from 21:00 the day before.

Antique furnishings, 1980s magazines left out to read, and a Frenc
places.chef: owner-operated cafe · Nara, Japan · Tucked into Nara's old Kitamachi district along the Yasuragi-no-Michi promenade, near the south gate of Nara Women's University, Bardot is a small owner-run coffee house that wears its Showa-era nostalgia proudly. Antique furnishings, 1980s magazines left out to read, and a French touch — red awnings, French flags, and a wall of Brigitte Bardot photos that gives the shop its name — set the mood, while jazz and bossa nova drift through the room. · The owners aim to offer guests a leisurely, unhurried stretch of time in an intimate setting, leaning into old-fashioned, nostalgic flavors rather than chasing trends. · The signature dish is the Kitamachi Napolitan: al dente spaghetti tossed with sausage, onion, bell pepper, and mushrooms in a rich tomato sauce, crowned with a fried egg and finished with parmesan and Tabasco. The café is also known for its soy-sauce ice cream — Uemura Farm ice cream drizzled with a special soy sauce from Oita (with a salt-topped version using Uyuni salt-lake salt) — and a Nara-only excavation-themed 'Kofun' dry curry served with a little shovel-shaped spoon. The cafe ole is made with unhomogenized Uemura Farm milk.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The signature dishes are wheat-based — the Kitamachi Napolitan is spaghetti and the dry curry is served with rice but the menu centers on retro café cooking with no documented gluten-free options or allergen accommodation. A celiac traveler should not rely on this kitchen.
places.vgd: Not a vegan destination. Signature items include sausage, fried egg, parmesan, and dairy-based ice cream (Uemura Farm milk), and there is no documented vegan menu. A flexible vegetarian might find a drink or a simple item, but anyone strict should ask in advance and not count on it.

places.chef: museum cafe, coffee and light meals, sweets and baumkuchen · Cafe Half Time sits one level below the galleries of the Nara National Museum, a quiet stop where you can pause between looking at Buddhist art and treasures of the old capital. places.chef: Kazuo Kita (喜多和夫) · owner · Nara, Japan · The building was raised in 1925 by Kazuo Kita's great-grandfather as the Chojukai Bacterial Research Institute, a factory that researched lactic-acid bacteria and produced a probiotic drink called 'Futurmin,' along with studies of edible fungi and bread yeast. It was designed by master carpenter Yoshitaro Oki, who also worked on Nara's Anglican church, and features hand-cut glass lamps by craftsman Koji Fujimoto. After the factory closed in the late 1970s it sat unused for more than three decades. · Kita's guiding idea was to preserve the building by using it — 'preserve it while it lives,' so visitors can feel an atmosphere that cannot be recreated in anything new. · Yamato tea and a weekend breakfast set, the much-loved croquette bread (a butcher's croquette with sweet sauce in fluffy bread, branded with a deer mark), fermented-butter toast, hojicha latte, and white dango.
places.gfd: This is a Japanese cafe built around bread, dango, and tea. Signature items — the croquette bread (コロッケパン), fermented-butter toast, sandwiches, and white dango (mochi rice flour) — are wheat- or gluten-containing, and there is no documented gluten-free menu or celiac protocol. Not suitable for strict gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: A drink-and-light-food cafe rather than a vegan destination. Plant-based options are incidental: Yamato tea (大和茶), persimmon-leaf tea (柿の葉茶), and a fig compote are vegan-friendly, but the hojicha latte and butter toast contain dairy and breakfast/lunch sets are not designed to be vegan. No documented vegan menu; ask staff about specific items.

places.chef: independent local teahouse / food stall · Nara (Todai-ji temple grounds, Zōshi-chō) · Rokumeien is a long-running, old-fashioned teahouse and food stall tucked into the wooded grounds of Todai-ji, on a quiet hill beyond the Great Buddha Hall near Nigatsu-dō. Surrounded by greenery in a free-to-enter part of the temple precinct, it has the unhurried, Shōwa-era character of a roadside tea shop — a place where visitors rest in the shade away from the crowds. · A focus on simple, handmade, locally sourced fare — pure ice with house-made syrups and Nara ingredients, served in a calm setting away from the tourist crush. · Home-made curry and curry udon with a dashi broth, seasonal curry nyūmen, house-made warabi mochi served with home-cooked red beans, and shaved ice (kakigori). The signature kakigori is a rice-themed bowl combining amazake syrup (made from rice), rice-flour dumplings, and concentrated red bean paste; the kinako (roasted soybean) milk ice with honey mizore is also a favorite, praised for fluffy, finely shaved ice and a clean, non-cloying finish.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The signature dishes — curry udon and nyūmen (thin somen-style noodles) — are wheat-based, and broths are dashi-based. No gluten-free menu or accommodations are documented. Not suitable for celiacs.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small machiya soba shop tucked into the historic Naramachi quarter near the Naramachi Shiryokan, Ginsho has been making soba in the neighborhood for around 32 years. Behind its nostalgic wooden lattice door and red noren, the room glows with warm lighting and Japanese knick-kna
places.chef: soba shop, tempura · A small machiya soba shop tucked into the historic Naramachi quarter (Nishi-Shinya-cho, near Sarusawa Pond and the Naramachi Shiryokan), Ginsho has been making soba in the neighborhood for around 32 years. Behind its nostalgic wooden lattice door and red noren, the room glows with warm lighting and Japanese knick-knacks, the kind of unhurried lunch spot locals have leaned on for decades. It is a branch of the family's main Ginsho shop over in the Takabatake area near Shin-Yakushi-ji. · The shop keeps things simple and fresh: noodles and tempura made to order, a bonito-dashi broth left largely unadorned to let the soba speak, and a willingness to keep going only as long as the day's hand-cut soba lasts. · Thin, fragrant soba made from stone-ground buckwheat flour, prized for its delicate texture and smooth throat-feel. The runaway favorite is tempura zaru soba — cold soba with crisp tempura (shrimp, pumpkin, eggplant, green beans, nori) fried to order — alongside tendon and a mini tempura rice bowl. The zaru is finished with a scattering of chopped nori, an unusual touch.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. The soba is nihachi (二八), an 80% buckwheat / 20% wheat-flour blend, so the noodles themselves contain wheat. Udon (pure wheat) is also offered, tempura is wheat-batter fried to order, and the broth uses soy-based tsuyu. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no allergen accommodation is documented. Unsuitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The soba dipping sauce and broth are made with bonito (katsuo) dashi, and the most popular dishes are tempura zaru soba and tendon. No documented vegetable-only broth or vegan options. A traveler could ask for plain zaru soba, but the standard tsuyu/dashi contains fish, so it cannot be assumed vegan.

The original exterior of the old machiya has been kept while the inside was renovated into a calm, surprisingly roomy space with a counter and table seating. · A 地産地消 (local-production-for-local-consumption) approach built around ingredients found only in Nara, run as a soba shop by day and a soba-and-sake izakaya by night. · Hand-cut soba made mostly from Hokkaido hikigurumi buckwheat flour with about a 20% binder, blended fresh each day to give thin noodles with a firm, chewy bite. places.chef: curry specialist · Wakakusa Curry Honpo sits just south of Kintetsu Nara Station, tucked into the Mochiidono covered shopping arcade that links the station area to the old streets of Naramachi. It is a compact, independent spice-curry house known for healthy, vegetable-forward cooking. · The shop's stated concept is building flavorful, nutritious dishes from abundant vegetables (such as spinach and tomato) and aromatic spices. · The house signature is the Wakakusa ('young grass') Curry, a spinach- and vegetable-heavy spiced curry, served alongside the shop's curry bread. The lineup spans a coconut-milk chicken curry, a mild Yamato beef curry that is popular with children, baked (yaki) curry, omelet (omu) curry, curry ramen, and a famously fiery lamb brown curry. The shop also lists vegetarian and vegan curries, along with gluten-free and pork-free options.
places.gfd: The official site states "gluten-free, pork-free menu options" are available, but no specific gluten-free dish is documented and there is no information on dedicated equipment or cross-contamination controls. Curry roux, curry bread (a signature item), and curry ramen are wheat-based, and the kitchen handles wheat heavily, so this is not a celiac-safe environment. Celiac travelers should ask directly about which curries are truly gluten-free and how they are prepared before ordering.
places.vgd: There is a genuine meat- and fish-free veg line: the Veg Wakakusa Curry (¥1,250), a sesame-and-vegetable curry made for vegetarians, with a version available without garlic or onion for Buddhist-style diets. Affectionately nicknamed 'Osha-kame' by regulars, it draws both Nara locals and visitors and has grown from an omurice specialist into a full casual cafe. · Everything is made by hand — from sauces to the kakigori syrups and pudding — with the master and his wife taking time and care to chase flavor rather than expand endlessly. · Fluffy, creamy omelette rice over chicken rice, served tableside so diners cut the center to reveal a silky half-cooked egg, with a choice of sauces (demi-glace, white sauce, and more) and toppings such as hamburg. Beyond omurice the menu spans pasta, doria, fried shrimp, pizza, parfaits, and seasonal shaved ice with homemade syrups and rich house-made jelly.
places.gfd: This is a Western-style cafe whose menu is built around wheat: omurice with demi-glace and white (roux-based) sauces, pasta, doria, pizza, fried shrimp, and hamburg. Such dishes are wheat- and flour-heavy and the kitchen makes no documented gluten-free accommodation, so it is not suitable for celiacs. No gluten-free menu or handling is advertised.
places.vgd: A meat-and-egg yoshoku cafe — the signature dish is a fluffy omelette over chicken rice, and other staples include hamburg steak, fried shrimp, and dairy-based sauces. places.chef: fruit growers, café operators · Nara (Yoshino) fruit orchard dating to the Meiji era · Horiuchi Kajitsuen grew out of a family fruit orchard in Nara and Yoshino that has continued since the Meiji era. The growers opened a storefront to show off the quality of their tree-ripened, seasonal fruit, starting on Sanjo-dori in central Nara, and have since expanded to Osaka and Tokyo. · Described as a shop where the farmers themselves propose ways to enjoy fruit: offering fresh, tree-ripened produce in a casual style, with the menu rotating according to what is in season and when each fruit is at its best. · Fruit sandwiches piled with fresh cream and ripe seasonal fruit (notably on a mildly sweet black-sugar bread), seasonal shaved ice made with fresh fruit (more than ten varieties in the May-October season), fruit zenzai, mixed juice and smoothies, stone-baked sweet potato, and a persimmon tiramisu.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The signature items are fruit sandwiches on wheat bread (including a black-sugar bread), so the core menu is wheat-based. There is no documented gluten-free preparation or allergy handling; smoothies, mixed juice, and stone-baked sweet potato may be naturally wheat-free but cross-contact is not addressed.
places.vgd: Largely not vegan. Headline items (fruit sandwiches, fruit zenzai, persimmon tiramisu) use fresh dairy cream and bread. Fresh fruit, mixed juice/smoothies, and the stone-baked sweet potato could be plant-based, but no vegan labeling or dairy-free options are documented, so confirm ingredients on site.

places.chef: cafe, bar, Nara-themed shop and event space · Central Nara (Nara City, Konishi-cho) · Tucked on the second floor of a small alley linking Konishi-dori and the Higashimuki arcade, just a minute's walk from Kintetsu Nara Station, this cafe-bar occupies the former home of a long-shuttered kissaten called Akadama. It is the second outpost of Fulucoto (Furukoto), a shop devoted to books and goods about Nara, and it doubles as a cafe, a small bar, a retail nook of Nara-themed wares, and a venue for cultural events. · Bringing the world of Heijo-kyo and the Tenpyo era to the table — naming dishes after historical figures and serving them in replica ancient vessels so guests taste Nara's deep history. · Ancient-Nara-themed treats: a rotating cast of kakigori shaved ice named after Asuka and Tenpyo-era figures (such as Ooshiama with Yoshino kudzu and homemade granita, Chujohime with loquat-leaf tea and lotus seeds, and Ichihiko with Asuka Ruby strawberry syrup), plus 'ancient sweets' sets like sakubei and magari, the fermented dairy delicacy 'so' said to echo ancient cheese, and house Mahoroba craft beers.
places.gfd: No gluten-free program is documented. Not suitable for celiacs without direct confirmation.

Secondary listings mention seasonal dairy-free, egg-free hotcakes and canelés in the colder months, but this is not stated on the official menu, so plant-based eaters should ask in advance. It keeps a retro, Showa-era atmosphere with a Japanese-style glass-door exterior that opens onto a homey dining room of a ha
places.chef: owner-operated neighborhood diner · Miyoshi is a long-established, unpretentious Western-style diner tucked into the historic Naramachi quarter, where most eateries lean expensive and trendy. It keeps a retro, Showa-era atmosphere with a Japanese-style glass-door exterior that opens onto a homey dining room of about five four-top tables, drawing both locals and visitors and often filling up at lunch. · The appeal is honest value and flavor over fashion: hearty, traditional yoshoku at modest prices in an area where that is increasingly rare. · The kitchen is known for its Yamato chicken (大和肉鶏, Nara's brand chicken) cutlet, described as tender and juicy, and for a hamburg in a rich, grown-up demi-glace sauce. Combination lunch sets pair hamburg, chicken cutlet, and pork saute, and other favorites include a generous beef cutlet set with rich demi-glace, a special omurice with thin egg and fried prawn and chicken, and a winter oyster-fry set. Sets come with salad, small side dishes, miso soup, and rice.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Western-style diner built around breaded, deep-fried dishes (chicken cutlet, beef cutlet, oyster fry, shrimp fry), hamburg with demi-glace, omurice, and curry — all wheat-heavy and not safe for celiacs. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
places.vgd: The menu centers on meat and seafood (Yamato chicken cutlet, hamburg, pork sauté, beef cutlet, fried oysters/shrimp), and set meals come with miso soup that typically uses fish dashi. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
places.hours: 10:30–19:00; closed Mondays (or the following day if Monday is a public holiday). Reported as currently lunch-focused, finishing around early/mid afternoon depending on the day.

places.n: ならまち 招福庵 (Naramachi Shofukuan)
places.hood: Naramachi (Nishishinya-cho)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Opened on New Year's Day, January 1, 2021, in a renovated town house in the heart of Naramachi, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. The proprietor greets every guest in full kimono and prepares matcha at the table.
places.chef: Toshiko Fukumoto · owner, host · Opened on New Year's Day, January 1, 2021, in a renovated town house in the heart of Naramachi, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. The proprietor greets every guest in full kimono and prepares matcha at the table. · The owner's wish is to offer a calm place where locals and travelers alike can relax over matcha and sweets, serving food that is both delicious and gentle on the body through traditional fermentation. · Naturally cultivated Yamato-tea matcha whisked tableside, homemade rice-koji amazake, and fermented red-bean anko. Signature items include a Matcha Set where guests choose their own Akahada-yaki tea bowl, a deer-themed matcha kakigori topped with four kinds of anko and a deer-shaped amber candy, and a sugar-free fermented-anko amazake zenzai.
places.gfd: Not a gluten-free establishment and no GF program is documented. The signature offerings — matcha, koji amazake, and red-bean anko — are naturally wheat-free, but the menu also includes mochi-based sweets and wagashi where wheat and cross-contact cannot be ruled out. A celiac diner would need to ask in person; nothing here is verified as celiac-safe.
places.vgd: Many core items are plant-based by nature: naturally cultivated Yamato-tea matcha, homemade rice-koji amazake, and sugar-free fermented-anko zenzai. However the cafe makes no vegan claim, and dishes such as the matcha kakigori include vanilla ice cream (dairy), so vegan diners should confirm which items are free of dairy and egg. Plenty of likely-vegan choices, but ask to be sure.

places.chef: 甘味処・喫茶, 日本茶・抹茶の提供, 茶道体験ワークショップ, 茶道具の販売 · 日本（奈良・ならまち） · 茶論（さろん）奈良町店は、奈良発祥の老舗・中川政七商店が手がける、茶道文化の入り口をテーマにした甘味処・喫茶です。ならまちの元林院町に残る伝統的な町家を生かし、床の間や季節の花、軸、手入れの行き届いた庭を備えた凛とした空間で、気軽にお茶と和菓子を楽しめます。 · 「茶道は敷居が高い」と感じる人にも、作法に縛られず気軽に一服を楽しんでほしいという思いから、スタッフが丁寧に手ほどきし、自分の手で抹茶を点てられるようにしています。茶道文化を身近に体験できる入り口でありたいという姿勢が貫かれています。 · 季節の和菓子と選りすぐりの日本茶、抹茶。喫茶では季節の和菓子と薄茶のセットのほか、自分で抹茶を点てる「自点て」体験、本格的なお茶席（季節の和菓子・濃茶・干菓子・薄茶）が用意され、夏には白いかき氷も供されます。テイクアウトの濃茶ラテなどもあります。
places.gfd: No gluten-free program is documented. A celiac visitor would need to ask about each item; cross-contamination is not addressed anywhere on the site.
places.vgd: This is a tea-culture café serving matcha, Japanese tea, and seasonal wagashi. Traditional wagashi and matcha are frequently plant-based (red bean, rice, sugar), so vegan options likely exist, but the shop publishes no vegan labeling. Seasonal sweets vary and some may contain dairy or egg, so a vegan visitor should confirm ingredients per item.

places.notes: Le Case (Italian for "the houses") opened in December 2011 in a renovated old folk house tucked inside Nara Park, surrounded by the wooded slopes of Kasuga Mountain and a short walk from Kasuga Taisha shrine. The shop is led by a chef who trained in Italy, and the building's tabl
places.chef: chef-owner · Nara, Japan · Le Case (Italian for "the houses") opened in December 2011 in a renovated old folk house tucked inside Nara Park, surrounded by the wooded slopes of Kasuga Mountain and a short walk from Kasuga Taisha shrine. The shop is led by a chef who trained in Italy, and the building's table seats and a back tatami room give it a quiet, lived-in feel. · The founder wants to show children how delicious vegetables can be, choosing ingredients that children can eat safely and that are high in nutritional value. Vegetables are organic and as much as possible grown within Nara Prefecture. · Seasonal savory and dessert quiches, with around fifteen colorful varieties lined up in the showcase. Signature quiches include onion (Cipolla), conger eel and burdock, scallop and lemon cream, and an apple ('white apple') quiche, plus a red-wine cheesecake. The tart dough is made with fertilized eggs, whole-wheat and rye flour, and fermented butter.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The tart crust is explicitly made with whole wheat (全粒粉) and rye (ライ麦粉) flour, both of which contain gluten. Quiche is inherently a wheat-pastry dish, so this is not suitable for celiac or gluten-avoiding diners.
places.vgd: Not vegan. Although the shop emphasizes organic Nara-grown vegetables, the quiche is built on eggs (有精卵/fertilized eggs), fermented butter, cheese and cream custard. Signature items include conger eel, scallop and red-wine cheesecake. No documented vegan options.

places.chef: Taro Sugimori · owner, chef · Naramachi, Nara City · Grill TALO opened in May 2023 on a quiet street in Nara's Naramachi/Kyobate district. places.chef: 畑 純平 (Hata Junpei) · owner, chef · Nara · The restaurant is run by Junpei Hata, born in 1974 in Nara. He first stepped into a kitchen as a part-time student cook, earned his culinary credentials, and worked his way up to managing local establishments before opening his own place to put Nara's regional ingredients in the spotlight. Today he largely runs the kitchen single-handedly. · A daily-changing menu driven by whatever vegetables, fish, chicken and local sake are best that day — a showcase for Nara's own produce and Yamato chicken. · The kitchen centers on three pillars named in the shop's own name: Yamato seasonal vegetables, Yamato meat-chicken (大和肉鶏), and local fish. The most talked-about dish is the 野菜刺身盛合せ — a platter of raw seasonal vegetables (carrot, eggplant, turnip, burdock and more) sourced from contract farms and served with a rotating choice of dipping sauces so each bite tastes different. places.chef: owner-chef, owner couple · A husband-and-wife soba shop opened in 1989 (Heisei 1) on a quiet stretch of Yasuragi-no-michi in central Nara, roughly midway between JR Nara, Kintetsu Nara and Kyobate stations. The entrance is so understated that regulars warn it is easy to walk straight past. The chef built the place on skills honed in Japanese cuisine and traditional soba-making, and after more than three decades it has become a settled, homey neighborhood fixture. · The kitchen works under the idea of shinmi-ushin (true flavor made with sincerity), pairing carefully blended buckwheat with a refined dashi drawn from bonito, round-herring (urume) flakes and Hokkaido Rausu kombu so the aroma of the soba comes through. · Hand-cut juwari (100% buckwheat) soba made from a custom Azumino Sarashina-style blend, served thin with an emphasis on smooth throat-feel. Signatures include zaru soba, oroshi (grated daikon) soba, kakiage soba, a limited daily wariko soba, and lightly fried seasonal tempura, finished with the house soba-yu.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free or celiac-safe. Although the house soba is described as juwari (100% buckwheat), the kitchen fries wheat-batter tempura and kakiage in the same small space, the dashi/dipping sauce is soy-sauce based, and there is no documented allergen control or dedicated equipment. Treat as unsafe for celiac.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The soba dipping/broth dashi is made from bonito (katsuo), aji/horse mackerel and Rausu kombu, so it contains fish; tempura and side dishes are not vegetarian-oriented. No documented vegan options.

places.chef: chicken specialist, izakaya · Nara · An independent chicken-focused izakaya near Kintetsu Nara Station, along the quiet Yasuragi-no-michi just off the Higashimuki shopping street. The kitchen builds everything around Yamato niku-dori (大和肉鶏), Nara Prefecture's prized brand chicken, sourced from a contracted poultry farm. · Staff travel to the poultry farm to pick up freshly dressed chicken each morning, prizing the breed for its sweetness, depth of umami, gentle springy texture, and balanced fat — fresh enough to serve raw. · Charcoal-grilled skewers of morning-fresh chicken, chicken sashimi and tataki made possible by the daily-procured freshness, the signature Yamato shirako (soft roe) with ponzu and grated momiji-oroshi, plus a chicken ramen and oyako-don to finish. House and seasonal Nara sake round out the table.

Grilled skewers are basted in tare (a soy-sauce-based glaze that normally contains wheat) and dishes such as the Yamato soft-roe ponzu use soy/citrus sauces that typically contain wheat. No gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or allergen accommodation is documented. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: A chicken specialist built around Yamato jidori — grilled skewers, chicken sashimi/tataki, soft roe, chicken ramen and oyako-don. The menu is meat- and fish-centered with soy- and dashi-based seasonings; there is no vegan offering or documented vegetable-only option.

places.chef: Toshihiro Matsuoka · owner · Satei Yusui sits at the very edge of Nara Park, at the foot of Mt. Wakakusa where the path into the Kasuga primeval forest begins. Run by owner Toshihiro Matsuoka, it is a small, green-surrounded teahouse-style eatery devoted to the old everyday foods of the Nara basin. · The kitchen frames its food as the bounty of Nara (奈良の恵ごはん) — a shojin-leaning, meat-, egg- and dairy-free way of cooking that leans on locally grown vegetables, rice and miso to express the taste of Nara through the seasons, from spring greenery to autumn leaves. · The house specialties are chagayu (rice gently simmered in roasted hojicha tea) and chameshi (tea rice cooked with roasted soybeans), served alongside Miwa somen and seasonal local-vegetable side dishes. Warabi mochi is whisked up fresh to order from genuine warabi (bracken) starch and served with kinako, sweet bean and black-sugar syrup.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. Core offerings are wheat-heavy: Miwa somen and udon are wheat noodles, and chagayu/chameshi use hojicha and likely soy seasoning. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no allergen/cross-contamination information is documented. A celiac traveler should not rely on this place.

It is the kind of resting spot where temple pilgrims and Nara locals have long stopped to ease the ti
places.chef: owner · A long-standing, modest teahouse tucked into the grounds of Todai-ji, sitting directly in front of the Sangatsudo and looking out through large windows toward the Nigatsudo hall. It is the kind of resting spot where temple pilgrims and Nara locals have long stopped to ease the tiredness of a stroll through the precincts. · While ornate multi-thousand-yen chagayu courses exist elsewhere, this teahouse leans into a humble, unadorned preparation, the kind that feels like what chagayu was always meant to be. · The signature dish is Nara-style chagayu (tea porridge): raw rice is slowly roasted in-house each morning until golden, then simmered in hojicha roasted tea into a light, fragrant porridge in which the natural sweetness of the rice comes through simply. It arrives with pickles and small side dishes — Nara-zuke, shibazuke, kombu tsukudani, umeboshi, and kiriboshi daikon — so diners can adjust the flavors to taste. Alongside the porridge the teahouse serves warm nyumen/somen, udon, soba and traditional sweets like zenzai.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The core menu is wheat-heavy — udon, soba (often containing wheat), and nyumen/somen are all wheat noodles, and pickles/sweets are typically prepared with regular soy sauce and dashi. The chagayu (tea porridge with rice) is itself wheat-free, but it is served with accompaniments (pickles, tsukudani) that commonly contain wheat-based soy sauce, and there is no indication of celiac-safe handling or a dedicated fryer. Treat as not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not a vegan destination. The chagayu (hojicha-roasted tea porridge with rice) and some pickled-vegetable sides (奈良漬, 柴漬け, 切り干し大根, 梅干し) are plant-based in themselves, but noodle dishes use fish/bonito dashi and the herring soba contains fish, so most cooked items are not vegan. places.chef: owner, soba chef · Nara (Naramachi area, central Nara) · Sobakiri Momoyozuki is a small, couple-run soba shop tucked into a quiet street within walking distance of Kintetsu Nara Station, recognizable by its wooden frame and large glass windows that open onto the kitchen. The owner shaped his craft under the influence of the renowned Osaka soba shop Sobakiri Bongu in the Taisho district. · The shop encourages diners to taste the noodles first with just salt -- 'mazu wa oshio de' -- to appreciate the buckwheat's inherent aroma and character before reaching for the dipping broth, which is kept restrained in sweetness so as not to overpower the textured noodles. · Stone-milled, hand-ground, hand-cut soba. The kitchen prepares both nihachi (80% buckwheat) and jūwari (100% buckwheat) noodles, with a hand-ground 100% buckwheat version limited to about ten servings a day. Buckwheat is sourced seasonally from regions such as Shimane (Matsue), Okayama (Hiruzen), Gunma, Hiroshima, Hokkaido and Fukui. Seasonal bukkake/tsukemen-style soba rotates roughly every two months from spring through autumn, with warm soba in the colder months, alongside side dishes and the soba-zenzai (buckwheat dumpli…
places.gfd: Not gluten-free or celiac-safe. While the headline jūwari (100% buckwheat) soba contains no wheat in the noodle itself, the menu also includes nihachi (80/20 buckwheat-to-wheat) noodles, and the dipping/broth tsuyu is made with standard soy sauce and dashi, both of which typically contain wheat. There is no dedicated gluten-free preparation, no separate boiling water, and no documented allergen handling, so heavy cross-contact with wheat is expected in a soba kitchen.
places.vgd: Not vegan. The soba is served with a tsuyu/broth based on fish dashi (described as a robust, restrained-sweetness stock), and seasonal specialties include duck-broth soba. Soy sauce is used throughout. No vegan options are documented.

places.chef: 西本 · owner, soba chef · Nagano Prefecture Togakushi buckwheat, stone-ground in-house · 蕎麦切り 西本 is a small, owner-run soba shop tucked into the西木辻町 corner of Nara between the historic Naramachi district and Kyobate, set slightly off the main tourist streets so it keeps a calm, neighborhood feel. The kitchen mills its own buckwheat on a stone mill (石臼挽き) using Togakushi buckwheat from Nagano Prefecture. · Generous, unfussy portions of freshly stone-ground soba in a quiet room, finished with thick, buckwheat-rich そば湯 poured over the dipping broth; local sake and soba-shochu are kept on hand for a leisurely meal. · The house style is Izushi-influenced 皿そば (plate soba) served as five small plates per person with egg and grated mountain yam on the side, alongside a rotating lineup of roughly seven cold and ten warm soba. Crowd favorites include the かき揚げ天ざる (vegetable-fritter tempura with cold soba), 鴨 (duck) cooked shabu-shabu style in a mushroom broth, あなご天 (conger-eel tempura, two generous ~15cm pieces), and a spicy soba made with the owner's home-grown purple daikon.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The soba is made in a 二八 (2:8) blend, meaning roughly 20% wheat flour is mixed into the buckwheat, and the dipping broth and warm soup contain wheat-based soy sauce. Tempura items (天ざる, かき揚げ, あなご天) are wheat-battered and fried. There is no indication of a dedicated gluten-free preparation or fryer, so this is not safe for celiac diners.
places.vgd: Not a vegan destination. The soba dough itself contains wheat (not animal product), but the standard tsuyu/broth is fish-dashi based and the soup soba and duck dishes use animal stock; some sets come with egg and grated yam. A plain cold ざる order without the dashi tsuyu could be near-vegan, but there is no documented vegan broth, so vegan diners would need to confirm in person.

places.chef: chef-owner · Tenri, Nara Prefecture · Yuki-tei began in Tenri City as Bistro Yuki-tei before relocating to Nara's historic Naramachi district in July 2012, settling into a bright, glass-fronted space near the Sugioka calligraphy museum. The chef trained for about twelve years in hotel restaurant kitchens, learning classic Western technique before opening his own place. · Everything possible is made in-house rather than from commercial products, including the slow-cooked demi-glace and the dressings, aiming for honest, approachable Western flavors that are rich but never overpowering. · Fluffy-creamy omurice: a softly set omelet draped over lightly sweet chicken rice, finished with a house-made demi-glace (or ketchup, by choice), served as a set with soup and salad. places.chef: husband-and-wife owners · Nara (Shimosanjo-cho) · A husband-and-wife team has quietly run this little soba house for more than twenty years, tucked into a calm side lane just off the bustle of Sanjo-dori, a short walk from the Nara stations. A small frog ornament marks the door, and the interior feels like an old farmhouse. · The menu is kept deliberately spare — essentially just mori and kama-age soba — because, as the owners put it, strongly flavored dishes would kill the taste of the noodles (味の強いものはそばの味を殺してしまう). The food is meant to let the buckwheat speak for itself. · Hand-pounded jūwari (100%) buckwheat soba made from 'kirishita soba' — sweet, fragrant buckwheat grown in the cool, mist-covered highlands — worked with no wheat binder at all. The signature mori soba is served drained on a thick wooden board rather than a bamboo basket, a presentation that depends on precise water-draining technique. Simple sides round it out: fifteen-grain rice porridge (十五穀かゆ), Nara-style persimmon-leaf sushi (柿の葉寿司), and mountain-vegetable inari, alongside a thoughtfully chosen lineup of local sake.

places.chef: 伊豫正純 (Iyo Masasumi) · founder, second-generation owner, udon artisan · The founder trained at his family's kamaage-udon restaurant in Miyazaki Prefecture before opening in Nara about 45 years ago. · Founded roughly four to four-and-a-half decades ago, Shigenoi began on a streetside spot and moved about 25 years ago to its current quiet alley near the station. The founder, now in his late seventies, still helps in the kitchen during the day, and his son Takehide took over as the second-generation owner several years ago. The shop has drawn families across two to four generations, plus fans who travel from afar. · The family aims to preserve both the shop's taste and its old-world atmosphere for the next generation; as Takehide puts it, the dashi is there to bring out the flavor of the udon. · Hand-made kamaage udon: noodles of just flour and salt water, hand-kneaded for an hour, foot-pressed for two hours, then rested for four — cut fresh to order so each strand varies a little in thickness. The dipping dashi, while primarily kombu/shiitake/bonito, accompanies wheat noodles, and no gluten-free preparation exists.
places.vgd: The signature dashi is made with three types of bonito (katsuobushi) in addition to kombu and dried shiitake, so the broth is not vegan. Complimentary lunch sides include inari-zushi and chirashi-zushi. There is no documented vegan option.

places.chef: 森田三和 (Miwa Morita) · owner, baker, cookbook author · Nara · MIA'S BREAD began roughly four decades ago from a small home kitchen and became a full bakery in 1997. Owner-baker Miwa Morita, who came to bread-making from a background in graphic design after baking as a hobby since high school, has run the shop through several Nara locations, returning to the Naramachi area in 2017 before settling in 2024 into a renovated old house in the Takabatake district, which Morita calls the shop's fourth and final chapter. Morita has published numerous bread- and sandwich-making cookbooks and essays. · Morita aims for bread with 'a gentle flavor you never tire of, a taste that lets you see a landscape,' made only from quality ingredients without additives, balancing the depth of natural sourdough with the lightness of yeast. · Thirty to forty kinds of additive-free natural-yeast and yeast breads daily — bâtards, baguettes, muffins, scones, and bagels — and a celebrated range of sandwiches: thick-cut toast sandwiches, soft non-toasted sandwiches, muffin and bagel sandwiches, pan-baked focaccia for sharing, and pita pockets. Several times a day the staff perform a breathtaking high-speed mochi pounding right at the storefront, drawing
places.chef: family-run wagashi shop, yomogi mochi maker · Founded in 1992 in central Nara by a man from the remote Kototsu district of Kamikitayama Village in Yoshino, who wanted to share his mountain hometown's traditional mochi with a wider audience. · Nakatanidou is a small family-run wagashi shop on Mochiidono shopping street, just steps from Kintetsu Nara Station, that has become one of Nara's most beloved sights. Several times a day the staff perform a breathtaking high-speed mochi pounding right at the storefront, drawing crowds who watch the mallet strike up to twice per second. · The shop insists the lightning-fast pounding is not a show but genuinely necessary work: pounding the rice while it is still piping hot keeps it from cooling and stiffening, yielding mochi that is at once soft, smooth, and beautifully stretchy. · Freshly pounded yomogi mochi (mugwort rice cake) filled with sweet red bean paste and dusted in kinako, made from carefully chosen ingredients: Saga Hiyoku glutinous rice, Hokkaido Tokachi red beans, domestic kinako, and fresh mugwort sprouts from Uwajima, Ehime.
places.gfd: The signature yomogi mochi is built on glutinous rice, mugwort, sweet red bean paste, and kinako (roasted soybean flour), so the core product contains no wheat by recipe. However, this is a small artisan stand with no published allergen program, no celiac handling, and shared equipment, so it is not verified celiac-safe — ask before assuming.
places.vgd: The yomogi mochi ingredients that are documented (Saga Hiyoku glutinous rice, Hokkaido Tokachi red beans, domestic kinako/soybean flour, Ehime mugwort) are all plant-based, so the main item appears to contain no animal products. There is no official vegan or allergen statement, so a strict vegan should confirm in person.

places.chef: owner-host, tea practitioner · Nara — the cafe pours teas grown in Nara Prefecture (Yamato tea), including roji sencha, naturally-grown sencha and black tea, kamairi-cha (pan-fired tea), and hojicha. · Utsugi is a small, individually run tea-and-art cafe tucked into the quiet southern edge of Naramachi. You take your shoes off at the entrance and settle into an intimate, wood-finished room built for slowing down. · The host's idea is to choose your tea and tea vessel according to your body and mood and brew it carefully for yourself — 体調や気分に合わせてお茶を選び、茶器を選び、自分の為に丁寧に淹れる. The space doubles as an art cafe, inviting reading, drawing, and writing while you sip. · A tea service (about 1,000 yen) where you choose a Nara tea to match your mood, brewed in an iron kettle (tetsubin) for three to five infusions and paired with a seasonal fresh wagashi (jō-namagashi). There are also dessert plates and glass drinks such as hojicha latte, roasted chai, and ginger ale.
places.gfd: No gluten-free claims are made anywhere on the cafe's pages. The menu centers on brewed Nara teas served with seasonal wagashi (上生菓子), dessert plates, and baked goods. Wagashi can sometimes be naturally wheat-free (rice/bean based) but baked goods contain wheat, and no allergen handling is documented. A celiac visitor would need to ask in person about each item; nothing here is verified safe.
places.vgd: No vegan labeling is documented. The core offering is tea (vegan by nature) paired with seasonal Japanese sweets; drinks include hojicha latte and chai (likely dairy), and dessert plates may include baked goods with eggs/dairy. Some wagashi are plant-based, but this is not verified per item. A vegan visitor should confirm the specific sweet and whether latte/chai use dairy milk.

places.chef: Ishikawa · owner · Opened on 2 November 2020 in a quiet corner of Naramachi by an owner named Ishikawa, an avid international traveler who wanted to bring the unhurried richness of overseas tea culture home to Japan. · To convey, in Japan, the abundance and slowness of tea time the owner experienced abroad, engaging all five senses through aroma, the mist of the kettle, and a space that blends Japanese and Western aesthetics. · Carefully brewed Yamato-cha, especially kabusecha (shaded tea) sourced directly from tea farmers in Nara's Tahara district, served as three successive infusions at different temperatures (the first drawing out umami, the second balancing umami and bitterness, the third a clean finish), and finished with ochitashi, the steeped leaves served as a small side. places.gfd: No gluten-free claims are published anywhere. This is a tea café whose food is sweets — the signature purple-sweet-potato Mont Blanc is built on a sponge base and chocolate crumble (wheat), so the menu is not celiac-safe. The tea itself (Yamato kabusecha) is naturally gluten-free, but no dedicated GF handling is documented. A celiac would need to confirm directly and likely stick to tea only.
places.vgd: The core offering is brewed Yamato tea, which is plant-based, and the tea is finished with an ochitashi (the steeped tea leaves served as a small side). However, the documented sweets (Mont Blanc with whipped cream, warabimochi) contain dairy, so they are not vegan. No vegan menu or substitutions are advertised. A vegan can enjoy the tea service but should ask about any food item.

places.chef: maker, tea house · Kamikitayama / Okuyoshino, Nara Prefecture · Izasa is the dine-in tea house of Nakatani Honpo, a Nara persimmon-leaf-sushi house that began in 1921 (Taishō 10) as a rice merchant, Nakatani Shōten, in the mountain village of Kamikitayama in Okuyoshino. Selling rice in a village that thrived on forestry, the family also sold the local kakinoha-zushi; about fifty years ago the previous owners devised their bamboo-leaf-wrapped 'Izasa-zushi,' and the company reinvented itself as a maker of Nara's regional 'specialty sushi,' reaching its 100th anniversary in 2021. places.chef: wagashi maker, family-run confectioner · Naramachi, Nara City · Kasuga-an is a long-established wagashi (Japanese confectionery) house in the historic Naramachi district, near Gangō-ji temple. Founded in 1897 (Meiji 30) and now run by the fourth generation, it has spent well over a century making and selling its signature satsuma-yaki, with a quiet second-floor tea room where visitors can rest and taste sweets fresh from the kitchen. · The house specialty is satsuma-yaki — a sweet-potato-shaped manjū. Smooth koshi-an (strained red bean paste) made from Hokkaido azuki and finished light and not overly sweet is wrapped in a thin dough kneaded from wheat flour and egg, then individually skewered on bamboo and grilled over direct heat to give it its characteristic browned, sweet-potato-like skin. The tea room also serves mochi, kuzukiri, warabi-mochi, and seasonal kakigori such as Yamato matcha shaved ice with red beans, paired with matcha, coffee, or tea.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The signature satsuma-yaki bun is made of a wheat-flour-and-egg dough wrapped around red bean paste, and the tea room serves wheat-based wagashi alongside mochi and warabi-mochi items. There is no indication of gluten-free options or celiac accommodation, and cross-contact with wheat flour is unavoidable in a wagashi kitchen.
places.vgd: Some items appear plant-based in principle (anko/red bean paste, kuzukiri, kuzumochi, warabi-mochi, matcha kakigori), but the signature satsuma-yaki contains egg in its dough, and no allergen or vegan information is published. A strict vegan would need to ask item-by-item; nothing is certified or advertised as vegan.

The Naramachi location was renovated and reopened on August 10, 2023, adding eat-in seating and seasonal menu items so visitors can enjoy the sweet potatoes on the spot in the atmospheric old-town setting. · The focus is on letting the sweet potato create its own natural, additive-free sweetness through long aging and careful roasting, drawing out a honey-like depth of flavor. · Their signature is the 濃蜜焼き芋『維新蔵の蜜芋』, a rich honey-like roasted sweet potato. places.chef: independent restaurant · Nara (Naramachi / Minamiichi-machi) · Kyoya began as an udon specialist on Nishi-Kitsutsuji before relocating into a traditional wooden townhouse in Nara's atmospheric Naramachi quarter, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station near Sarusawa Pond. places.chef: Masahiro Someya · founder, egg craftsman · Nara, Japan · Someya Shoten began about 70 years ago as a specialist workshop making thick-rolled egg for the sushi trade. Founder and master craftsman Masahiro Someya, now in his 80s, supplied gyoku (sushi-topping egg) and sweet datemaki egg rolls wholesale to fish markets and sushi restaurants. As the family workshop's members aged past 70 and questions of succession and physical strain set in, the family decided to preserve the craft in a new form, converting the ground floor of their three-story former workshop-residence in Naramachi into a small cafe one summer. · The founder's eldest daughter Kiyoko, who now runs the cafe, describes the aim that customers remember their dashi-maki tamago so warmly they would want to taste it one more time. Ingredients are sourced locally: eggs, Koshihikari rice, Yamato (Nara) vegetables, and domestic bonito and kombu for the broth. · Dashi-maki tamago (dashi-rolled omelet) teishoku set meals; also a thick egg sandwich and classic omurice. The signature omelet is built around about four eggs and a generous amount of dashi for a soft, fluffy texture, cooked fresh to order.
places.gfd: Not a gluten-free destination. The signature dashi-maki tamago and set meals rely on Japanese dashi and seasonings that typically include wheat-based soy sauce, and rice is served alongside. No gluten-free protocols are documented, so a celiac diner would need to ask directly and exercise caution.
places.vgd: Not vegan-suitable. The core offering is egg-based (dashi-maki tamago, egg sandwiches, omurice) and the dashi is made from bonito (katsuo) and kombu, so it contains fish. No vegan options are documented.

places.chef: tea house, sweets shop (甘味処) · Nara, Japan · Yanagi Chaya was founded in 1902 (Meiji 35) beside Sarusawa Pond, in the shadow of Kofukuji's five-story pagoda in central Nara. It was opened specifically to keep alive Nara's old tea-rice tradition: 'nara chameshi' (奈良茶飯), rice cooked with tea and roasted, crushed soybeans, a dish eaten in Nara since ancient times that had been fading from memory. The shop occupies a wooden building that has stood since the Meiji era, and visitors are seated in tatami rooms, at tables, or in private rooms looking out toward the pond. · Preserving Nara's tea-rice culture so that it would not be forgotten, served in a historic wooden tea house overlooking Sarusawa Pond. · Warabi mochi (bracken-starch jelly served with matcha) is the flagship, available year-round; there is also a milk warabi mochi variation with red bean and chestnut, and seasonal kakigori (shaved ice with strawberry or Uji kinako). The founding signature is the nara chameshi set.

Vegan-leaning diners should ask which sweets are free of dairy; this is not a dedicated vegetarian/vegan destination.

places.chef: eel specialist restaurant · Naramachi, Nara · The restaurant occupies a roughly 150-year-old former merchant house in the heart of Naramachi. Built in the Meiji era, it was owned by the Miyajima family, who ran a kimono and textile shop here for generations—its latticed itoya-goshi facade still signals that fiber-trade past. After the shop closed in 1985, the building was carefully converted into a dining house, keeping original details such as a wooden box-staircase (hakodansu) that is still in use, along with sunken-hearth-style seating. · The kitchen follows the old eel-cook's creed, 'three years to skewer, eight years to fillet, a lifetime to grill,' and continually replenishes a founding tare said to carry more than seventy years of accumulated flavor. · Tokyo (Kanto)-style eel: the fish is split along the back, skewered and white-grilled, then steamed to render out fat and finished with a second grill, so it turns soft, fluffy and lighter in fat. Signature dishes include unaju/unadon over rice with a long-aged kabayaki sauce, and hitsumabushi served so you can enjoy it three ways.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. places.chef: Okabe Ayako · owner, cook · Tagawa City, Fukuoka Prefecture (founder's hometown, source of the shop name) · Kissa Tagawa opened in 1966 in Nara's Kitamachi district and has been a beloved neighborhood fixture for over half a century. The shop's founder hailed from Tagawa City in Fukuoka Prefecture — the source of the shop's name — where he had run a bicycle shop before moving to Osaka to work as a bartender and in the coffee wholesale trade, where he met and married a woman from Tenri in Nara. places.chef: Kamimura Masao (上村政雄) · owner, chef · Kōchi Prefecture · Sunbird is a one-man omurice specialist run by owner-chef Kamimura Masao, originally from Kōchi, who built up roughly two decades of experience at ethnic-cuisine restaurants and cafes in Nara before opening his own omelette-rice shop. He cooks alone, which can mean a wait at busy times. The shop opened in Naramachi in 2017 and relocated on September 20, 2022 to a quieter second-floor space in the Kitamachi (きたまち) area near Nara Women's University, where it has built a loyal base of local regulars. · An emphasis on carefully sourced local Nara ingredients: specialty free-range eggs from Ōmiya Farm in Kashihara, Igeta soy sauce from the long-established Inoue Honten, and after the move a switch to fragrant, chewy Nara-grown Hitomebore rice. · The signature dish is the lemon butter soy sauce omurice — fluffy egg over soy-based chicken rice finished with a house sauce made from lemon, butter and Igeta soy sauce. places.chef: Vietnamese kitchen · Vietnam · Com Ngon is a Vietnamese restaurant tucked up a narrow staircase on the second floor of a building in the Higashimuki shopping arcade, a few minutes' walk from the center of Nara, with a soba shop occupying the floor below. places.chef: confectioner, sweets parlor · Nara, Japan · A long-established Nara confectioner founded in the Meiji era (1898, Meiji 31), said to have started as an independent venture after splitting from the Osaka house of Tsuruya Hachiman. The main shop sits in the Shimomikado arcade (Shimomikado-cho 29) at the northern edge of Naramachi, and after a 2022 renovation that added a tea room it continues to draw locals and visitors for both takeaway sweets and an in-shop sweets-parlor experience. · A confectioner rooted in Nara's classical imagery, naming and shaping sweets after the ancient capital's poetry and history. · The house signature is 'Aoniyoshi,' an elegant two-toned strip confection. Once made like rakugan from rice flour, it was reworked using kudzu starch, giving it its distinctive delicate texture. In summer the shop is loved for its kakigori: shaved ice with wasanbon-sugar syrup, black molasses, and house-made red bean paste from premium large azuki, finished with decorative leaf candies; a salted cherry-blossom 'sakura-gori' is also offered. Year-round the cases hold anmitsu, the imperial-style 'Kenjo Mikasa' filled cakes, monaka, yokan, senbei, and castella.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. This is a traditional wagashi shop whose core products are wheat-based: castella, mikasa (dorayaki-style filled cakes), monaka wafers, and senbei all contain wheat flour. While the signature kakigori (kuzu/wasanbon syrup over shaved ice with house-made azuki bean paste) and pure-azuki items may be naturally low in wheat, the kitchen handles wheat-based confections extensively, so there is no dedicated gluten-free preparation and high cross-contact risk. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not advertised as vegan. Many items are plant-based by tradition (azuki bean paste, kuzu, agar/anmitsu, the signature aoniyoshi rakugan-style sweet made from kudzu starch and sugar), but the shop also makes egg-and-dairy confections such as castella and sponge-based mikasa, and does not label items for vegans. A vegan traveler could potentially eat plain anko-based sweets, the aoniyoshi, or fruit…

The second generation, Yamamoto Kenji, grew the business, and since 1998 the third generation, Yamamoto Tetsuya, has led the shop, now in its ninth decade in Nara. · The shop aims to create sweets, spaces, and hospitality that make the heart quietly calm — what they call 'おだやかな幸せ' (calm happiness). · Fresh warabimochi (生わらび餅) — a melt-in-the-mouth bracken-starch sweet dusted with kinako. The standard version blends domestic bracken starch with sweet-potato starch; the top-grade 純本生わらび餅 uses 100% domestic bracken starch with only sugar and water, hand-kneaded by veteran artisans. A historic candy called 古代瓦 (ancient roof tile) is named for the imagery of Todaiji and Nara's old architecture.
places.gfd: The house specialty is warabimochi, traditionally a wheat-free confection. The standard version blends sweet potato starch with domestic bracken (warabi) starch; the premium "pure" warabimochi (純本生わらび餅) uses 100% domestic bracken starch with only sugar and water. So the core sweet contains no wheat. However, it is dusted with kinako (roasted soybean flour) and the shop publishes no gluten-free or cross-contamination guarantees, and other wagashi sold here may contain wheat. Celiacs should ask d…
places.vgd: The signature warabimochi is plant-based: bracken/sweet-potato starch, sugar, water, and kinako (soybean flour) topping, with no animal products in its core recipe. This is a confectionery shop, not a vegan-focused destination, and ingredient lists vary by item (some wagashi may use eggs or dairy). No formal vegan menu or cross-contact policy is documented, so vegans should confirm individual ite…

It opened on November 24, 2025, in the space formerly occupied by 'Kissaten Mickey,' a cafe long loved by the local community, and was reborn as a collaboration between the Shinroku kissaten concept and Tokyo-based OSHIMA DONUTS. places.vgd: The core offering is fried wheat donuts (typically made with egg, dairy and butter) and coffee. No vegan menu or plant-based options are documented, and the parfait/coffee drinks would normally use dairy. Not a vegan destination.

places.chef: Wagashi maker, Confectioner · Nara, Japan · Tsuruya Tokuman is one of Nara's long-established wagashi (traditional Japanese confectionery) houses, founded in 1898 (Meiji 31) and associated with the older Nara Tsuruya (Tsuruya Hachiman) confectionery lineage, with a craft tradition the house describes as spanning well over a century. The shop sits on the old Mochiidono / Sanjo arcade streets in the heart of Nara, between Kintetsu Nara and JR Nara stations. · The house emphasizes traditional methods and Nara's regional confectionery heritage, taking pride in long-standing craft; its mikasa has been presented to the imperial household on multiple occasions, commemorated by a thank-you plaque from Kashihara Shrine displayed in the shop. · The signature product is the 三笠 (mikasa) — a generous dorayaki-style pancake about 13cm across, made with large premium adzuki beans and a moist, fluffy batter, with a celebrated 'kenjo mikasa' version. places.gfd: This is a traditional Japanese-sweets maker. Its core products are wheat-based: the signature 三笠 (mikasa / dorayaki) is made with wheat flour, eggs and honey, and other baked confections similarly use flour. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no allergen labeling for celiacs, and no separate preparation. Not suitable for those requiring strict gluten-free.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Chef Tsuyoshi Akeboshi trained at established Japanese restaurants and well-regarded hotels before opening this small shop in the historic Naramachi district in 2011. He runs it together with his wife as an intimate, reservation-only counter-and-tables eatery.
places.chef: 明星剛志 (Tsuyoshi Akeboshi) · owner-chef, husband-and-wife team · Naramachi, central Nara · Chef Tsuyoshi Akeboshi trained at established Japanese restaurants and well-regarded hotels before opening this small shop in the historic Naramachi district in 2011. He runs it together with his wife as an intimate, reservation-only counter-and-tables eatery of about 12 seats. · A health-minded, ingredient-first approach: the finest Yamato Pork cooked gently to highlight its natural sweetness, balanced by an abundance of vegetables and digestive teas before and after the meal. · Tonkatsu made from Yamato Pork (a premium Nara-prefecture brand pork prized for tender meat and sweet, oleic-acid-rich fat). The pork is coated in coarse panko for a light, crisp finish and fried gently in soybean oil at a low temperature (around 160C). It is served not with sauce but with Guerande sea salt from France blended with sweet tea, herbs, and the shop's own spices. Sets come with a heaping plate of cabbage, a vegetable-laden soup, a seasoned side, and rice blended with barley, Job's tears, and legumes; the meal opens with mekabu tea and closes with black oolong tea.
places.gfd: This is a tonkatsu (breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet) specialist. The signature dish is coated in wheat-flour panko breadcrumbs and is not gluten-free. The accompanying vegetable soup and seasoned sides typically rely on standard dashi and seasonings, and the set rice is blended with barley (a gluten grain). There is no documented gluten-free menu or celiac-safe preparation, and no dedicated fryer. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: A pork specialty restaurant built entirely around Yamato Pork cutlets, ginger-grilled pork, pork steak, and katsu curry. While the meal includes a notably generous amount of vegetables (a heaping plate of cabbage and a vegetable-rich soup), the soup contains imitation crab and the dishes are not prepared as vegan/vegetarian. No plant-based main is documented. Not suitable for vegans.
