places.chef: owner-operated independent cafe · あしゅーら occupies a roughly 100-year-old machiya (traditional townhouse) tucked into the quiet southern edge of Naramachi, near Kyobate. The old wooden interior is dressed with Indian and Asian crafts and a faintly temple-like, oriental atmosphere, giving the room the feel of a hideaway rather than a busy cafe. · A meat- and fish-free kitchen built on organic, pesticide-free vegetables and brown rice. The mood is deliberately unhurried — guests summon the easygoing owner by ringing a bell or tapping a wooden fish block, and are even told they are welcome to doze off after eating. · The signature plate is a brown-rice (genmai) vegetable curry. The Calcutta-style sauce gets its depth from pesticide-free onions caramelized slowly and beans blended smooth, so it tastes rich without any meat or fish. A popular variation adds 'gluten' (seitan made from wheat flour) that is crisped up to mimic chicken. Other regulars include tofu croquettes, omurice, soup spaghetti, papad, plus a tea menu with chai and fresh carrot juice and house-baked scones.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free or celiac-safe. A signature dish is "gluten curry" made with seitan (wheat gluten, グルテン, made from flour to mimic chicken), and the menu includes other wheat items (scones, omurice, spaghetti, papad). Despite the word "gluten-free" appearing in some third-party listing snippets, the kitchen actively uses wheat gluten and is not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: Vegetarian establishment using no meat or fish. Many dishes are genuinely vegan (the bean/onion-based curries use no animal products, and dishes without egg, milk, or yogurt are available on request). However, it is not fully vegan: the spicy curry sauce can include yogurt (dairy) for sweetness/tang, and omurice/omelette dishes use eggs. Vegans should specifically ask for egg-, milk-, and yogurt-…

places.chef: Sugimoto Yuta · owner, host · Naramachi, Nara (Hanazono-chō) · Nishimura-tei occupies a Nara machiya (traditional wooden townhouse) more than 100 years old that opened to the public in autumn 2019. The owner, Sugimoto Yuta, graduated from university in Tokyo and worked at a graphic-design company and then in food-service before returning to his hometown and renovating the family house — his grandmother's home — keeping the original stairs, beams, and two gardens, into a guesthouse with a small café and rental space at the quiet southern edge of Naramachi. · The kitchen aims for food you could eat every day without tiring of it — gentle on the body and quietly nostalgic, evoking the comfort of a grandmother's home. The whole place is built around an 'obāchan-chi' (grandmother's house) feeling of unhurried rest. · The signature dish is the 'everyday tea-rice set' (毎日の茶飯膳): rice cooked with local Nara hojicha roasted tea, miso soup, seasonal vegetable small dishes, and Nara pickles (also offered vegetarian/vegan), with an optional homemade rolled egg ('okan no tamagoyaki') as an add-on. The café also serves coffee, tea, and sweets sourced from local Nara shops, plus seasonal items li…
places.gfd: No documented gluten-free program. The café centers on rice-based dishes (hojicha-cooked rice, miso soup, seasonal small plates, Nara pickles), and a homestyle rice meal can be relatively low in obvious wheat, but miso, Nara pickles (often soy/koji-based), and any soy seasoning may contain wheat, and there is no stated celiac/cross-contamination protocol. Galettes and breads on the menu contain gluten. A celiac traveler must ask directly (info@nishimuratei.com / SNS) before relying on it.

places.chef: 大八木もえ（Moe Oyagi） · owner · Nara · ROKKAN ROOM occupies a townhouse more than 140 years old in Motobayashiin-cho, once the heart of Nara's old flower district just south of Sarusawa Pond. The building was formerly an okiya (a residence for geisha), and owner Moe Oyagi actually lived in it before reimagining it as a café. She kept the layers of its past intact: the original earthen-floored entry, a storehouse (kura), repurposed lacquer tables from the okiya, and a wartime air-raid shelter in the basement now softened with tatami and cushions. · Cooking around the themes of fermentation and spice using local Nara ingredients, herbs and medicinal touches, while preserving and celebrating the building's many historical layers through a deliberately eclectic old-meets-new design. · Nyūmen made with Nara's local Miwa sōmen, served with a spiced fried-tofu pouch that releases curry when broken open; a chai-infused zenzai (red-bean soup) layering cinnamon, ginger and clove over strained sweet beans; and a custard pudding made with Nara-prefecture eggs.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The signature nyūmen is made with Miwa sōmen (wheat noodles), and the menu features curries and a custard pudding. No gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or celiac accommodations are documented; broths almost certainly contain wheat-based seasonings and the place is not set up for cross-contamination control.
places.vgd: Not a vegan venue. Some dishes appear plant-leaning (spiced fried-tofu nyūmen, chai-infused red-bean zenzai), but nyūmen broth is typically made with fish dashi and curries are not confirmed animal-free; the pudding uses Nara eggs. A flexible vegetarian might find an item by asking, but vegans should not assume any dish is safe without confirming dashi and curry ingredients.

places.chef: owner-roaster, owner's wife (baker) · Nara, Japan · TABI Coffee Roaster opened on July 18, 2017, tucked inside the retro Tsubai Market (椿井市場) arcade a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. The owner spent roughly 11-13 years training as a roaster at the well-known Nara coffee house Kuroko before striking out on his own, and he runs the stand together with his wife, who hand-bakes the pastries. · A focus on careful, small-batch hand-roasting using fully hand-picked premium beans, aiming to make fresh, approachable coffee that appeals to a wide range of ages. · House-roasted single-origin and blend coffees, including the signature TABI Blend (a deeper roast with pronounced bitterness and depth) and a medium-roast version, plus rotating single origins. The shop is small-batch and hands-on: the owner hand-picks world-class green beans to remove defects, then roasts in small lots from medium to dark. His wife's homemade canelé and biscotti accompany the coffee.
places.gfd: A specialty coffee stand, not a gluten-free destination. The only food offered is the owner's wife's homemade baked goods (canelé, biscotti), which are wheat-based. No gluten-free items or celiac handling are documented. Coffee itself is naturally gluten-free, but there is no dedicated GF preparation.
places.vgd: This is primarily a coffee stand. Black coffee is plant-based, but milk-based drinks use dairy and no plant-milk option is documented. The accompanying baked goods (canelé, biscotti) typically contain eggs and dairy. No vegan menu or labeling exists; a vegan visitor would need to stick to black coffee and ask about any food.

places.chef: owner · A small, independently run Japanese cafe tucked into a quiet lane near the Nara Hotel on the southern edge of the old Naramachi district. It pairs casual creative Japanese cooking with house-made sweets in a relaxed, homey setting, and welcomes guests with pet-friendly outdoor terrace seating on fine days. · A focus on local Nara ingredients and seasonal home-style cooking, refreshed frequently so regulars find something new. · The standout is the 'Wanzu Heart no Gohan' plate (around 1,400 yen): a main dish with several small seasonal sides, miso soup and pickles built around Nara-grown vegetables and locally produced Hinohikari rice. A playful 'grown-up's children's lunch' adds fried chicken and fried shrimp with house-made tartar sauce, and a distinctive Yoshino kudzu 'udon pasta' offers a slippery, chewy noodle in a crab-tomato cream sauce. Menus rotate roughly every two weeks with the seasons.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. Signature items include fried shrimp and chicken (wheat batter) and a kudzu-udon pasta dish; an official allergen note for the lunch lists shrimp, wheat and eggs. Soy sauce and miso here are standard wheat-containing types, so it is not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: This is a homestyle Japanese cafe whose signature plates feature fried chicken, fried shrimp, fish, miso soup and egg-based items. No vegan menu is documented and dishes rely on standard Japanese seasonings and likely fish dashi, so it is not a vegan destination.

places.chef: Yoshiro Wakita · owner, patissier · Nara (Takahata-cho) · Owner-chef Yoshiro Wakita trained as a chief patissier before opening his own shop in Takahata-cho, a quiet residential pocket at the foot of Kasuga Mountain where cake shops were scarce. The location took several years to ready, partly because deer wandering over from nearby Nara Park kept eating the greenery during the build. · Wakita aims for 'lightness' in everything, and wants the shop to be an 'air-like presence' that quietly stays close to people's hearts, using carefully chosen local Nara ingredients, fresh eggs, and milk from pasture-raised dairy farms. · The signature 'air cake' — an ultra-light dome of airy castella-style sponge wrapping a soft milk mousse (with red-bean paste), made in flavors such as plain, matcha (Uji green tea), orange (Ehime mandarin confit), and blueberry cheese. Other favorites include a Kotoka local-strawberry tart on a cookie-style crust and seasonal fruit cakes.
places.gfd: This is a cake and baked-goods shop. The signature "air cake," rolls, tarts, sponge cakes, cookies, and sablés are all built on wheat flour, so the menu is fundamentally not gluten-free. No gluten-free items or dedicated GF preparation are documented. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: The shop's cakes are made with fresh eggs and milk (the owner specifically highlights using fresh eggs and milk for the delicate texture), plus dairy mousse and butter-based pastries. No vegan/plant-based items are documented. Not suitable for vegans.

places.chef: owner · Nara (Kitamachi) · A small, family-feeling parlour in Nara's quiet Kitamachi district, just north of Kintetsu Nara Station. The owner fell for Okinawan culture and built the shop around 'yachimun' — Okinawan pottery with roughly 700 years of history — personally traveling to Okinawa to buy pieces directly from about ten different kilns. Those thick, rounded, hand-painted bowls, said to reflect the warmth of Okinawan people, are the vessels the desserts are served in. Although the owner was a beginner at shaved ice when opening, they developed a signature fluffy, snow-soft texture. · Recreate the feeling of sitting in a neighborhood Okinawan teahouse in the middle of Nara — gentle Ryukyuan music, handmade pottery, and island ingredients turned into playful, beautiful sweets. · Creative Okinawan-inspired kakigori served in handmade yachimun bowls: passion fruit and acerola from Motobu balanced with black sugar and custard, ice scented green with fuuchiba (Okinawan mugwort) for an aromatic, gently herbal note, and toppings like Okinawan senbei; seasonal cakes and fruit tarts round out the menu.

A celiac visitor would need to ask in person about each item.

places.chef: owner-baker · Japan (Nara) · A small artisanal bakery in Nara's quiet Takabatake district, on the south side of Nara Park near the temples and Kasuga Taisha approach. It opened in May 2009. The whimsical name 'Nomokemana' is the Japanese word for sloth, 'namakemono,' spelled backwards, and the shop carries a little sloth mascot to match — a nod to its slow, unhurried approach to bread. · Bread made slowly and honestly: domestic wheat and house-cultured natural yeast, with whole-grain flour worked into every loaf for rustic, deeply aromatic results. · French-style hard breads and a signature pain au levain raised with wild yeast cultivated from Ikoma-grown grapes, giving it a gentle tang. Around 30 kinds of bread are baked daily, from baguettes and walnut campagne to Japanese favorites like anpan and melon pan and French sweets such as kouglof. All loaves are blended with whole-grain flour milled from organically grown, pesticide-free wheat.

places.vgd: A natural-yeast bakery. places.chef: tea stand, persimmon-leaf grower and maker · Nara (Gojo City origins; persimmon leaves grown on the company's own organic farm in Tenri City) · KAKIHA started in 2014 as a tiny six-seat counter shop in Gojo City, southern Nara, devoted to the leaves of the persimmon tree. places.chef: restaurant · Naramachi, Nara · Harishin occupies a roughly 250-year-old machiya townhouse, formerly a money-changer's (両替商) shop, in the historic Naramachi quarter on the west side of the World Heritage temple Gangoji. The house faces the ancient 'Kamitsumichi' road (上ッ道) that once linked Fujiwara-kyo and Heijo-kyo and served as a pilgrimage and trade route during the Nara period. · Cooking that draws on Nara's history and local Yamato ingredients, served in a preserved Edo-era merchant townhouse so guests experience old Naramachi alongside the food. · Yamato regional cuisine highlighting Nara ingredients: the Kamitsumichi bento, the milk-based Asuka hotpot (飛鳥鍋, by reservation), tempura set meals, and the revived ancient cheese 蘇 (su), alongside Yamato vegetables like Yamato-mana and Yoshino kuzu and persimmon vinegar.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Yamato cuisine restaurant serving set meals (tempura set, bento, the Asuka milk hotpot) that rely on soy sauce, fish/chicken dashi and wheat-based items; the Asuka hotpot is even finished with udon (wheat). No gluten-free menu or allergy program is documented, so it is not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Dishes center on chicken, fish, dashi, eggs and the ancient dairy-based cheese 蘇 (su); the signature Asuka hotpot uses chicken broth and milk. While it features Yamato vegetables and Yoshino kuzu, no vegan or vegetarian menu is documented and most dishes use fish or chicken stock, so it is not a vegan destination.
places.hours: Lunch 11:30-15:00 (last order 14:00), Dinner 18:00-21:00 (last order 19:30). Closed Mondays (or the following day if Monday is a holiday) and Thursday evenings.

places.chef: owner · Kameya is a long-running okonomiyaki and teppanyaki institution that opened in 1965, just a short walk from Sarusawa Pond along the approach toward Sanjo-dori. More than half a century on, it remains a family-style neighborhood spot, recognizable from the street by its big red lantern and packed with a mix of local families, after-work groups, and visitors who have wandered up from the pond. · The shop describes its own draw simply as a distinctly flavored okonomiyaki and negi-yaki experience — straightforward griddle cooking meant to be enjoyed casually with a beer. · The house signature is the Daibutsu-yaki ('Great Buddha grill'), a jumbo negi-yaki just under 40cm across that has been on the menu for over 20 years. places.gfd: Not gluten-free in any form. places.chef: family-run, independent seafood izakaya · Central Nara, near JR Nara Station · A long-standing, family-run seafood spot tucked into the Sanjo-honmachi blocks barely a minute from JR Nara Station. It works like a neighborhood catch-of-the-day kitchen: the menu flexes with whatever fresh fish comes in that morning, so regulars come back to see what is good today rather than to order a fixed list. · Buy fresh, cook simply, change the menu with the day's catch — value and freshness over flash. · Fresh fish in every form — generous sashimi, grilled and simmered fish, and fried-fish sets. Lunch is the local draw: an excellent-value daily set (around 1,000 yen) that can include a beef main, simmered sea bream, sashimi, small dishes, rice, soup and pickles, plus a famous Tuesday-only special seafood donburi (yellowtail and salmon in sesame sauce topped with flying-fish roe).
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation documented. This is a Japanese seafood izakaya built around soy sauce, fish dashi, tempura/fried fish, and simmered dishes — all typically wheat-containing — so it is not safe for celiac diners. Sashimi exists but is served with regular (wheat-containing) soy sauce, and there is no dedicated GF handling.
places.vgd: This is a seafood restaurant; nearly every dish centers on fish or uses fish dashi. No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented and the kitchen is not set up for plant-based dining.

places.chef: family-run neighborhood Chinese restaurant · Nara · Shanhairo has been serving the Higashimuki shopping arcade just steps from Kintetsu Nara Station since 1945 (Showa 20), making it one of central Nara's longest-running Chinese restaurants. It keeps the unmistakable Showa-era machi-chuka character, with bright red tables on the ground floor and an upstairs banquet room that seats groups of up to about thirty. · Straightforward, orthodox cooking that lets genuine skill speak through familiar dishes rather than flashy specialties. · Honest, classic Chinese home cooking: generous-value lunch sets, mapo tofu, sweet-and-sour pork, shrimp in chili sauce, crab omelet, egg fried rice, and almond tofu for dessert. Most of the regular menu (apart from the noodles) is also available to take out.

places.chef: bakery, cafe, pizzeria · Nara · An offshoot of Chateau d'Or, a Nara bakery founded in 1972 that has been baking for more than fifty years. places.vgd: No vegan menu or labeling is documented. The menu centers on bread (typically containing egg/dairy/butter), cheese pizzas (e.g. Quattro Formaggi), egg-topped morning sets, seafood/chicken ajillo, beef curry donut and whitebait pizza. A traveler would need to ask, and plant-based options are not confirmed.

It has been running for over a decade and operates in three parts through the day: lunch, an afternoo
places.chef: owner-chef, husband-and-wife team · Naramachi, Nara City · Bambuno is a husband-and-wife-run creative Italian restaurant in a renovated 100-plus-year-old machiya townhouse in Nara's old Naramachi quarter, a short walk from Sarusawa Pond. It has been running for over a decade and operates in three parts through the day: lunch, an afternoon cafe, and dinner. · Local sourcing and community: the kitchen builds dishes around organic vegetables from its own kitchen garden and Nara-prefecture ingredients, with the stated idea that local encounters turn into deliciousness that makes people happy. · Its signature 'Naramachi Pasta' is a cream pasta made with sake lees from the local Harushika (Harushika Brewery) daiginjo, paired with Nara-brand Yamato Pork, seasonal local vegetables and grated ginger. 'Pasta Yamato' (with roasted-tea/hojicha flavor) and house-made bagna cauda also feature. During cafe hours the kitchen serves an unusual vegetable shaved ice known as 'Veji-gori' (ベジ氷), such as a tomato-and-apple shaved ice and a taro-and-ruby-chocolate version.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly: the signature dishes are wheat pasta (奈良町パスタ, パスタ大和) and there is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergy protocol. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Primarily an omnivore kitchen built around Yamato pork, cream and cheese, so it is not a vegan destination. However, it leans heavily on its own organic Nara vegetables and the cafe-time vegetable shaved ice ('ベジ氷') is vegetable-forward; some vegetable dishes may suit vegetarians. Vegans should call ahead and ask, as no formally vegan menu is documented and dairy/animal stock are common.

places.chef: owner-chef (itamae), proprietress (okami) — front of house · A long-established sushi shop tucked into the old streets of Naramachi, said to have been going for more than 70 years. The owner-chef works the counter alone, hand-pressing each piece and choosing the day's fish himself, while his wife runs the warm front-of-house service. · An unhurried, ingredient-first counter where everything is made by one pair of hands — service can be slow at busy times precisely because the owner refuses to rush the food. · Hand-pressed nigiri and an unusually generous chirashi (tuna, squid, yellowtail, shrimp, scallop, salmon, sea bream, eel — and, distinctively, simmered kōya-dōfu tofu over shiitake-and-egg-ribbon rice). places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. This is a traditional sushi restaurant where soy sauce (wheat-based) is used throughout, and the lunch menu prominently features udon (wheat noodles). Sushi rice is seasoned with vinegar but the prep, dashi-based simmered items (e.g. simmered anago, kōya-dōfu) and shared kitchen carry high gluten cross-contact risk. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans. As a sushi restaurant, virtually every dish centers on raw and cooked fish/seafood, and broths/simmered items rely on fish dashi. Even the chirashi's tofu sits atop fish-based ingredients. No vegan menu or accommodation is documented.

places.chef: independent café-restaurant · Pinocchio is a long-running, old-fashioned individual coffee shop (kissaten) in central Nara. It originally stood on Sanjo-dori, where it became known as a filming location for anime and dramas, before relocating into the historic Mochiidono shopping arcade a few minutes' walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. · Though it bills itself as a café, it is really a place to settle in for a proper meal and linger over coffee while watching the flow of people through the arcade. · The signature dish is the omurice: thin-cooked fluffy egg wrapped over chicken rice with onion and mushroom, served in classic, nostalgic style with variations such as cheese and seafood. The kitchen also turns out a wide range of hearty plates including curry doria, cod-roe cream pasta, hamburger rice bowls and pizza, plus homemade desserts like chiffon cake, baked and rare cheesecake, and chocolate cake.
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation. The menu centers on wheat-based dishes (pasta, pizza, breaded/fried items) and omurice is made with egg over chicken rice; sauces such as demi-glace typically contain wheat. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: No vegan options documented. Signature omurice uses egg and chicken; pasta, doria and most dishes rely on meat, seafood, dairy and egg. No plant-based menu found.

places.chef: Hiroki Kawabata · chef, owner-operator (Ashibiya Honpo) · Naramachi, Nara · cervo bianco opened in June 2018 inside a renovated Edo-period machiya (traditional townhouse) in the heart of Naramachi. It was created by Ashibiya Honpo, a long-established Nara pickle (narazuke) maker founded in the late Edo period, as part of an effort to bring new life to the old neighborhood. The wood-fired stone oven sits where the house's old bathhouse once stood, and its chimney is a surviving piece of that original structure — Western cooking quietly folded into a Japanese home. · An 'Enjoy NARA Flavor' concept — celebrating local Yamato produce, dairy, and tea through Italian technique, with the white-deer motif (the name means 'white deer' in Italian, after the legend of a deity arriving in Nara on a white stag) running through the artwork and dishes. · Wood-fired pizza and house-made gelato built around Nara-prefecture ingredients. The signature pizza, named after the ashibi (馬酔木) plant, pairs local narazuke pickles with four cheeses (mozzarella, gorgonzola, camembert, grana). places.chef: tea shop, kakigori cafe · Ochanoko is a small specialty tea shop on the Konishi-sakura shopping street in central Nara, tucked into the ground floor of the CoMoLLE (コトモール) building a couple of minutes from Kintetsu Nara Station. It began as a graduate of Nara's 'Yume Cube' (夢CUBE) startup-incubator program and grew into a beloved neighborhood spot. Alongside its retail tea counter it runs a small cafe known for shaved ice served all year round. · A focus on authentic, additive-free tea and on sharing reicha's tradition of hospitality, paired with shaved ice whose signature is an airy texture that 'melts away the moment you eat it.' · The shop's identity rests on three teas — locally grown Yamato (Nara) tea, Taiwanese tea sourced from leading Taiwan producers, and reicha (擂茶), a Hakka 'hospitality tea' blending more than twenty kinds of beans, grains, and green tea into a powdered drink, made additive-, color-, and fragrance-free. Its best-known cafe items are fluffy, quick-melting shaved ice with house-made grown-up syrups: original reicha ice, hojicha latte ice, and Asuka Ruby strawberry-milk ice, with add-ons like ice cream and walnut mochi.
places.gfd: No gluten-free program is documented. The signature reicha (擂茶) is a blended powder of 20-plus beans, grains, and green tea — grains may include wheat or be cross-contaminated, and shaved-ice syrups and toppings (e.g., walnut mochi) are unverified for gluten. A celiac traveler must ask about each item; treat as not confirmed gluten-free.
places.vgd: Teas themselves (Yamato tea, Taiwanese tea) are plant-based, but the cafe's headline items are dairy-based: hojicha latte ice and strawberry-milk ice use milk, and toppings like ice cream and mochi vary. Plain tea is fine for vegans; the shaved-ice and latte menu generally is not unless a dairy-free option is confirmed by asking.

places.chef: fresh pasta, creative pizza, café & bar, wine · Central Nara, Mochiidono shopping street · A tucked-away Italian spot on the second floor of a building along Nara's historic Mochiidono shopping arcade, a few minutes' walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. The café-bar sits within a select shop stocked with vintage clothing and homeware, so the dining room carries a warm, retro feel filled with cute bric-a-brac. · The stated idea is 'casual yet authentic Italian you can enjoy anytime' — approachable cooking and good wine in an unpretentious, welcoming room. · Hand-style fresh pasta is the heart of the kitchen — thick, springy noodles in dishes like a rich carbonara with chunky bacon, cream and cracked pepper, and a spicy amatriciana. places.chef: family business, specialty fish-cake shop, eat-in counter · Nara, Japan · Uoman was founded in 1901 (Meiji 34) and has operated for more than 120 years as a kamaboko and satsuma-age (fried fish cake) specialty shop in the heart of the Mochiidono Center-gai arcade, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. In landlocked Nara, the founding family built a reputation for bringing the nutrition and honest flavor of fish to the local table. · Balancing long tradition with playful innovation in fish-paste products, while honoring the value and taste of fish in a prefecture far from the sea. · Original surimi (ground-fish) creations: classic kamaboko and satsuma-age plus inventive fried items, most famously the 'butter potato' fish cake — potato and butter wrapped in a samosa sheet so it fries up crisp without the butter leaking. The shop fries items fresh at an open counter so customers can eat them piping hot, and offers walk-and-eat bites like one-mouthful 'NeRi Ball'.
places.gfd: This is a fried fish-cake (satsuma-age/kamaboko) shop. Surimi-based fried products typically contain wheat starch/flour binders, are deep-fried in shared oil, and are commonly served with soy sauce (which contains wheat). There is no indication of gluten-free preparation or a dedicated fryer; not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: The entire product line is fish-based (surimi kamaboko and satsuma-age made from ground fish). There are no vegan options; even the "butter potato" item is a fish-paste product. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: independent owner-operated lunch eatery · Nara, Japan · ごはんの間 opened in February 2011 in Nara's Kitamachi (Hanashiba-cho) area, a short walk north of Kintetsu Nara Station. From the street it looks almost like an ordinary house, opening only at midday and offering just that day's set meal. The room is plain and narrow, running long toward the back with two-person tables and counter-style communal seating that makes it easy to drop in alone. · A deliberately limited model -- lunch only, a daily-changing set menu -- that lets the kitchen keep meals affordable and generous without cutting corners on quality or comfort. · The daily-changing set meal (honjitsu no teishoku). The main dish rotates among home-style favorites such as vegetable and shrimp tempura or stuffed cabbage rolls, served with rice, miso soup, salad and a side. The rice is sourced from Tahara in Nara Prefecture and is singled out by diners as genuinely delicious, and the tempura oil is described as light and easy on the stomach.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The daily set centers on tempura or spring rolls (wheat batter/wrappers), and Japanese set meals here use standard soy sauce and miso, so wheat and gluten are present throughout. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans. The single daily set typically includes meat, seafood (e.g., shrimp tempura) or fried dishes, and the miso soup and seasonings use fish-based dashi. There is one fixed menu daily with no documented vegan option.
places.hours: 11:00-14:00 (lunch only). Closed Wednesday and Friday per Tabelog; an owner-blog source lists 11:00-15:00 closed Wednesday only, so closing time and Friday closure may vary.

places.chef: restaurant · Nara · Opened in 2012 in a renovated old machiya (traditional townhouse) in central Nara, with thick old beams that carry a sense of history, the place is built around a single beloved idea: rice done properly. The dining room is intimate, seating only around twenty, and the rhythm of the day is split in two — a relaxed, affordable kayaku-rice lunch and a quieter evening of sake and small dishes. · An obsession with rice quality — milling fresh for each batch and cooking it gently in dashi so the grains, not the seasoning, are the star. · Kayaku rice (mixed rice) is the centerpiece. The kitchen sources rice from a single farmer in Omihachiman, keeps it in a refrigerated case and mills only what is needed for each cooking so the rice is always fresh, then cooks it in a clay pot with kombu-and-bonito dashi. The result is described as elegant and subtle, never heavy, and is served in bent-wood boxes; lunch sets pair it with a protein such as tender-simmered chicken thigh and side dishes, while a popular dish is the kayaku-rice grilled rice ball served as ochazuke.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The signature kayaku rice is cooked in kombu-and-bonito dashi and seasoned with soy sauce (which contains wheat), and the izakaya-style dishes rely on standard Japanese seasonings. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented, and there is no indication of celiac-level cross-contamination control. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The house dashi uses bonito (katsuo) and the kayaku rice and set meals center on fish/meat dashi and animal proteins (e.g., tender-simmered chicken thigh). No vegan menu is documented; a strict vegan would have very little to eat. At most one could ask, but expect fish dashi throughout.
places.hours: Lunch 11:30-14:00 (L.O. 13:30; lunch ends when the kayaku rice sells out). Dinner 17:30-22:00 (last entry 20:00, L.O. 21:00). Closed Sundays and national holidays.

places.chef: Miyaka Hisashi · owner, chef · Naramachi (Nishi-Terabayashi-cho), central Nara, a few minutes from Sarusawa Pond. · Kinari Pizza is the solo project of Miyaka Hisashi, who trained as a baker in France and Italy before opening this open-air pizzeria in the heart of Naramachi. The shop is built around a distinctive white kitchen truck fitted with a wood-fired oven, with terrace seating and covered tables tucked behind it. · The owner deliberately built the stand with no door, saying he wants people to drop by casually (「ラフに遊びに来てほしいから扉は作らない」). places.chef: souvenir hall, group-tour restaurant, cafe, local-sake bar · Operated by World Heritage Co., Ltd. (ワールド・ヘリテイジ), based in Nara. · Nara Nagomi-kan sits in the Takabatake quarter on the edge of historic Naramachi, near Nara Park. Built to blend with the old town, its exterior wears ash-gray plaster walls echoing the weathered ink-gray of traditional local houses, and the entrance is guarded by a striking ascending-dragon sculpture carved from three Japanese pine logs as a symbol of prosperity and welcome. Inside, it is one of the prefecture's largest souvenir halls, stocking a broad range of Nara specialties and Japanese goods, alongside a large dining room for tour groups, a casual cafe, and a local-sake bar. · To gather Nara's specialties and food culture under one roof and welcome travelers in a setting designed to harmonize with the historic townscape. · Nara confectionery, especially mikasa (the local name for dorayaki) and other regional wagashi and sweets, plus an in-house sake bar pouring Nara local sake.
places.gfd: No gluten-free program is documented. This is a souvenir-and-cafe complex serving Nara wagashi such as mikasa (dorayaki) and assorted sweets, which are wheat-based, plus a tour-group restaurant menu likely relying on wheat-containing soy sauce and dashi. Celiac travelers should treat it as not gluten-free unless staff can confirm specific items; ask directly.
places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented. The cafe and group restaurant serve general Japanese fare and sweets; most Japanese dishes here likely use fish dashi, and wagashi may contain egg. places.chef: Kikuno (菊乃) · owner, active geiko (geisha), host · Naramachi (Imagomon-cho), Nara · Tsuruya is run by Kikuno, an active geiko, and is described in local press as the only surviving ochaya (geisha tea house) still run by an active geiko in Nara, set in a historic building with a vermilion-lacquered counter and period furnishings. places.chef: Kira Shinichiro (吉良 慎一郎) · head chef, manager · Nara Prefecture · Head chef and manager Kira Shinichiro was born in Nara Prefecture in 1973 and first stepped into the 一条 (Ichijo) kitchen as a student working a part-time job at the group's original izakaya. places.chef: sake merchant, standing bar / kakuuchi · Naramachi, central Nara · Founded in 1868 (Meiji 1), Ogawa Matabee Shoten is a long-established sake merchant standing in front of the World Heritage temple Gankoji in Nara's historic Naramachi quarter. Its storehouse is a nationally registered tangible cultural property and a designated Nara City landscape-preservation building (House No. 4), and a roughly 60-meter rail track once used to move sake barrels still runs inside. · The shop playfully sums up its mood as nurui (lukewarm), yurui (loose) and ayashii (mysterious) — an unhurried oasis for travelers wandering Naramachi, where you can sip while gazing at the temple across the street. · A curated lineup of Nara local sake said to gather bottles from breweries across the prefecture (around 70 varieties), served by the glass alongside craft beer and wine. Notable pours include a revived Taisho-era Sakura Beer and craft-beer flights.

places.vgd: This is a drinks-focused standing bar (local sake, craft beer, wine) rather than a kitchen; only light snacks may be available and none are documented as vegan. Sake and most beer are plant-based, but any food offerings and serving practices would need to be confirmed in person.

places.chef: owner-operated independent cafe · Nara, Japan · Anne-Marie Cafe is a long-running British-style cafe just a one-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station, at the entrance to the historic Kitamachi quarter (Higashimuki-Kitamachi). It opened around 1999 and has been loved by both locals and visitors for over two decades. The interior is done in an English-countryside style, and the cafe deliberately keeps a quiet, settled atmosphere so that even someone dropping in alone feels at ease. · A calm, welcoming English-style tearoom where guests — including those dining solo — can relax over scones and tea. · The house-made scones are the signature draw — served warm with clotted cream and jam, with a rotating range said to span dozens of seasonal varieties (around 60). Alongside the scones, the kitchen is known for its quiche, finger sandwiches, morning sets, and an afternoon tea set (from 14:00) that brings together sandwiches, quiche, pickles, cake, a scone of the day, marinated fruit, and a mini parfait/ice cream.
places.gfd: A British-style cafe whose menu centers on wheat-based items — scones, quiche, finger sandwiches, cakes. The cafe states that allergy accommodations are possible (アレルギー対応も可), so a gluten-sensitive diner could ask, but no flour-free dishes are confirmed.
places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented. places.chef: owners · Nara · PEAKS BEIGNET is run by the Okubo couple, who spent about two years selling their beignets at pop-up and temporary locations -- including 'Unso' on Mount Ikoma and the Nara venues 'Kore Kara' and 'SLOW HOUSE NARA' -- before opening this permanent shop in May 2021 in the quiet Takabatake neighborhood of southeast Naramachi. · A slow, unhurried cafe experience: they renovated the ground floor of a former vacant house into an intimate space and serve the beignets hot from the fryer so guests can enjoy that crisp-then-fluffy texture at its best. · Made-to-order beignets: a French-born, American-raised square fried pastry like a hole-less doughnut that puffs up balloon-like when fried, crisp on the outside and hollow and croissant-like inside. places.chef: irori charcoal grill, Yamato beef specialist, Naramachi dining · Naramachi, central Nara · A charcoal-grill dining room tucked into the historic Naramachi quarter, just in front of the east gate of Gangō-ji Temple. places.chef: Hiroshi Ida (井田弘) · chef, owner · Tottori Prefecture, Japan · Chef Hiroshi Ida, born in 1975 in Tottori Prefecture, trained in the kitchens of major Osaka hotels including Hotel Agora and Hotel Seagull, and spent five years as executive chef at Garden City Club Osaka before becoming the inaugural head chef of the DINING ROOM IN THE NARAMACHI in 2018. places.chef: family-run, owner-operated · A family-run Chinese diner that opened in 1977 in a quiet residential pocket of Nara's Kiji-machi neighborhood, just south of Naramachi. The shop's name comes from the owner's eldest son's name. Inside, a red-toned room holds a short counter and two round tables, with a worn, vintage feel and an old TV in the corner — a genuine slice of Showa-era Japan that draws a loyal crowd of local regulars. · Holding prices steady and the recipes unchanged for more than four decades — affordable, consistent, everyday food for the neighborhood. · The signature dish is the gyoza: ten crisp-edged pork-and-vegetable dumplings that have famously stayed at 300 yen since the day the shop opened. Beyond that, the kitchen turns out stamina ramen, fried rice, mapo-tofu rice bowls, sweet-and-sour pork, shrimp dishes, and around eleven affordable set meals served with rice and miso soup — the broad, comforting repertoire of a classic Japanese town Chinese restaurant.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free in any way. This is a classic town Chinese restaurant whose core menu is built on wheat: ramen, gyoza (wheat-flour wrappers), and fried rice and stir-fries seasoned with regular (wheat-based) soy sauce. There is no gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no indication staff accommodate celiac needs. Not safe for celiac or gluten-sensitive diners.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The signature gyoza are filled with ground pork, set meals center on meat, egg, and seafood (sweet-and-sour pork, shrimp dishes, chive-and-egg stir-fry), and ramen broth and stir-fries rely on animal-based stocks. No documented vegan or vegetarian options.

places.chef: independent izakaya · Mangyoku occupies one of the oldest surviving townhouses in Naramachi, a building dating to 1742 that once housed the geisha establishment known as Bangyokuro (萬玉楼) in the old Motorinoin-cho flower district. The wooden structure survives largely in its original form, and the interior keeps period touches such as antique water shelves and tansu chests, giving the small izakaya a quietly historic, grown-up atmosphere. · A refined, calm space for adults to linger over good sake and carefully made seasonal dishes within a centuries-old machiya. · Home-style Japanese small plates and izakaya fare meant to pair with sake: fluffy crab dumplings in a gentle broth, a soft dashi-rolled egg infused with shiitake and kombu, root-vegetable shira-ae (lotus root, burdock, carrot), roasted eggplant, steamed Hakata-style chicken, uni tofu and beef stew. The kitchen is noted for caring about its fish.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Japanese izakaya whose menu is built on fish/kombu dashi, soy sauce, and dishes such as dashi-rolled egg and sōmen (a wheat noodle). places.vgd: Although there are vegetable-forward small plates (e.g., root-vegetable shira-ae with lotus root, burdock and carrot; roasted eggplant), the kitchen is described as "particular about fish" and the cuisine relies on fish/bonito dashi. Signature items include crab dumplings, dashi-rolled egg, steamed chicken and beef stew. No vegan menu or vegan dashi is documented, so it is not a vegan destination…

places.chef: ryotei (traditional fine-dining house), kaiseki restaurant, wedding and banquet venue · Nara, Japan · Kikusuiro is a long-established ryotei founded in 1891, set just before the first torii gate of Kasuga Taisha at the edge of Nara Park. For more than 130 years it has welcomed prominent figures, intellectuals, and literary writers, becoming one of Nara's most storied dining houses. Its formal gate, relocated from Enjo-ji temple and dating to the Edo period, is a Registered Tangible Cultural Property, so guests step through a piece of preserved architectural history on their way in. · Hospitality and flavor refined through tradition, with care taken so that a meal can be enjoyed with all five senses - from delicate presentation down to the lingering aromas of each dish. · Seasonal kaiseki with no fixed menu - the head chef composes a unique course each day around the season and the guests. Signature touches include a carefully hand-ground sesame tofu (goma-dofu) and, for celebration courses, a whole roasted sea bream symbolizing good fortune, all made with Nara's seasonal produce.

The restaurant does state that allergy and dietary requests must be communicated at least 3 business days in advance, so a strict gluten-free traveler should arrange this far ahead and not assume safety. Treat as not celiac-saf…
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian by default. Goma-dofu (sesame tofu) is a documented signature, but that alone does not make the menu plant-based. The kitchen accepts dietary/allergy requests with at least 3 business days…

places.chef: owner, pastry chef, sweets-class instructor · Japan (Nara, Kitamachi) · A small Cake & Bread Cafe tucked into Nara's historic Kitamachi quarter, a short walk north of Kintetsu Nara Station. It is run by a woman who grew up in Kitamachi and returned to open her shop in the very neighborhood she calls home. Before baking professionally she worked as a kindergarten teacher, then became a cooking-school instructor and ran her own dessert classes, eventually turning that passion into this little storefront. · The owner likens making cakes to classical music, a quiet passion that deepened over the years, and says her aim is simply to offer sweets that bring a smile to every customer, each one made carefully and by hand. · Handmade cakes and baked goods made one at a time, with a rotating daily selection of roughly five to seven cakes, a few kinds of焼き菓子 (baked sweets) and breads, plus black tea, flavored teas and herbal teas you can enjoy in the small cafe space. Signature pieces include seasonal whole cakes, decorative flower cakes, macarons, and a tea-flavored chiffon cake.
places.gfd: This is a flour-based patisserie and bakery; cakes, breads, and baked goods are made with wheat flour and there is no documented gluten-free offering. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: A traditional Western-style bake shop whose cakes, breads, and baked sweets rely on butter, eggs, and dairy. No vegan or plant-based items are documented.

places.chef: dining bar, cafe · Nara, Japan · ヤマトモダン JR奈良駅前店 is a modern Japanese dining bar and cafe just a few minutes' walk from JR Nara Station, set in a townhouse-style space (it previously operated under the name 大和CAFE). It is part of a small family of Nara restaurants alongside やまと庵 and 大和野菜と串焼きやまと, all built on the same idea of cooking with local Nara-prefecture ingredients. · The concept is local-ingredient cooking by day and a casual bar by night ('夜はバル'), pairing Nara produce, pork and beef with regional sake such as Harushika from the Imanishi Seibei brewery. · The kitchen centers on Nara brand ingredients: Yamato pork spare ribs glazed in a sweet teriyaki sauce, Nara-style chicken nanban topped with pickled daikon, a Yamato beef mille-feuille cutlet, hand-made curry pizza, and an eggplant-and-red-miso bolognese. A daily vegetable platter showcases Yamato vegetables, and the daytime cafe is known for fluffy rice-flour (米粉) pancakes served scone-style with maple syrup, fresh cream and plenty of fruit.
places.gfd: No dedicated gluten-free program. The rice-flour (米粉) pancakes are naturally lower in wheat but are made in a shared kitchen with no documented allergen controls — treat as not safe for celiac without asking in person.
places.vgd: Not a vegan or vegetarian destination. It is an omnivore Nara-ingredient dining bar built around Yamato pork, Yamato beef and chicken. A vegan would need to ask the staff…

places.chef: owner-operated cafe, crepe specialist · Central Nara, Higashimuki-kita shopping arcade · A small, owner-run two-story cafe tucked into the Higashimuki-kita covered shopping street, just steps from Kintetsu Nara Station. The first floor has a counter where guests can chat with the owner, and the upstairs room offers relaxed sofa seating. It shifts gracefully through the day as a morning spot, a lunch cafe, and a casual evening place for a drink. · An additive-free, made-from-scratch approach to the crepe batter, aiming for honest, body-friendly food served in a warm, conversational setting. · Hand-made crepes are the heart of the menu, with more than ten savory and more than ten sweet varieties. The batter is made only from a blend of domestic bread and cake flour, milk, eggs, unsalted butter, and granulated sugar, with no additives, giving it a chewy texture. The fruit-laden dessert crepes (mango, kiwi, strawberry, banana) are a favorite, and lunch sets pair a crepe or short pasta with salad, soup, and a mini dessert. Hojicha and matcha lattes round out the drinks.
places.gfd: The house specialty is crepes made from 100% domestic wheat flour (a blend of bread flour and cake flour); pasta is also on the menu. These are wheat-based, so the cafe is not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten-free diners. No gluten-free options are documented.
places.vgd: The signature crepes are made with milk, eggs, and unsalted butter, and the sweet menu is dairy- and chocolate-based, so the core offerings are not vegan. No vegan menu or plant-based substitutions are documented.

places.chef: 紺木 邦廣 (Kunihiro Konoki) · owner, chef · Nara City, Shin-Omiya neighborhood · Yofu-dokoro Kon is a small owner-run Western-style eatery in Nara's Shin-Omiya district, a short walk from Shin-Omiya Station. places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian options are documented. The menu is built around meat and seafood (hamburg steak, fried chicken, fried shrimp, chicken/shrimp gratin) and dishes use meat-based demiglace; nothing on the official site or articles indicates plant-based dishes.

Sitting directly across from Hannyaji Temple in the quiet Kitamachi area north of central Nara, the roughly 1,800-tsubo farm stil
places.chef: family-run dairy farm, cafe-restaurant, farm shop · Nara (general) · いちづ is the cafe-restaurant of Uemura Bokujo, Nara's oldest dairy farm, run by the Uemura family since the Meiji era. Sitting directly across from Hannyaji Temple in the quiet Kitamachi area north of central Nara, the roughly 1,800-tsubo farm still keeps around 30 dairy cows alongside miniature horses, and delivers some 1,500 bottles of low-temperature pasteurized milk across Nara each day — including to the historic Nara Hotel. · The name 'Ichizu' means devoting oneself single-mindedly to dairy farming — a one-track dedication to good milk and the food made from it. · Western-style home cooking made with the farm's own fresh milk: cream croquette lunch, hamburg steak lunch, a mixed lunch, omelet-rice sets, and milk-based sweets — soft-serve ice cream, mochi ice cream, cookies, madeleines and financiers from the farm shop. The kitchen is led by a chef with experience at the Nara Hotel.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. The Western-style menu centers on wheat-heavy dishes — cream croquettes, hamburg steak, omelet rice and the farm's own cakes, cookies, madeleines and financiers. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no documented allergen accommodation. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. This is a dairy-farm restaurant whose entire identity is built around its own fresh milk, plus eggs and meat (hamburg steak, cream croquettes, omelet rice, parfaits, ice cream and milk-based sweets). Dairy and animal products are central to nearly every item; there are no documented plant-based options.
places.hours: 11:00–17:00 (14:00–17:00 cafe service only; lunch orders generally until ~14:00). Closed Wednesdays. (Sources also list 11:00–16:00; afternoon hours are cafe-only.)

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, independently run niboshi (dried-fish) ramen specialist tucked into central Nara, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station and about ten minutes from JR Nara. As the name suggests, dried fish is the heart of everything here.
places.chef: independent ramen shop · A small, independently run niboshi (dried-fish) ramen specialist tucked into central Nara, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station and about ten minutes from JR Nara. As the name suggests, dried fish is the heart of everything here. · A single-minded focus on dried fish — every bowl is designed to deliver a powerful, unmistakable niboshi punch. · The signature is a richly concentrated niboshi ramen built on a double broth that marries dried fish from across Japan — large sardine (ōba iwashi), urume, and aji — with a chicken paitan base. The deluxe special bowl (特製にぼこいラーメン) piles on six slices of chashu, a soft-boiled egg, menma, scallion and naruto, with fish powder over the nori to push the dried-fish character further. The shop also serves tsukemen (dipping noodles) in 200g, 300g and 400g portions, with house-made noodles.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The ramen and tsukemen noodles are wheat-based (the house noodles use a blend of two Hokkaido wheat varieties with tapioca starch), and the broth is built on fish niboshi and chicken with seasonings that typically include wheat-containing soy sauce. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan. The entire menu is built on a double broth of dried fish (large sardine, urume, aji) and chicken paitan, topped with pork chashu and egg. There are no vegan options.

places.chef: family/owner-run kissaten · A long-running classic kissaten near JR and Kintetsu Nara Stations, Rich has been pouring coffee and serving Western-style comfort food for around 40 years, occupying the ground floor of the Tokyu Dwell Nara Park Village building near the former Nara girls' high school along Sanjo-dori. · An unhurried, at-home (アットホーム) atmosphere that keeps decades of regulars coming back while staying easy for first-time visitors to drop into. · The house signature is a fluffy omurice — soft, half-set scrambled egg over ketchup rice with beef, mushrooms and onion, finished with a sweet demi-glace sauce. The other star is the coffee: a house blend of several beans brewed by siphon for a smooth, mellow, mild cup. Morning sets (egg sandwiches, toast) and lunch sets of curry, doria, gratin and pasta round out the menu, each lunch coming with salad, a mini dessert and a drink.

places.chef: wagyu beef specialist, sukiyaki restaurant · Nara, near Kintetsu Nara Station in the Higashimuki shopping arcade area · A Yamato-beef sukiyaki house created to turn a trip to Nara into lasting memories, conceived around the idea of reimagining the dining of Japan's ancient capital — when the region was called Yamato — in a contemporary way. · To convey the charm of Nara through sukiyaki, expressing respect for the region by showcasing local Nara ingredients in cuisine that echoes ancient imperial dining traditions. · Premium Yamato beef sukiyaki using A4-ranked female cattle of a heritage Nara breed documented as prized since the Kamakura period and sourced from Nara's Nakao Ranch, simmered in a house-made broth of aged soy sauce, dried shiitake and kombu; and gyu-mabushi beef rice bowls featuring seared beef tataki, shigure-ni style, and grilled loin. places.chef: 坂本節夫 (Setsuo Sakamoto, founder, deceased) and Miriam (his French wife) · owner, baker, host · Takabatake, Nara · A long-loved retro coffee house in Nara's quiet Takabatake neighborhood, near Nara University of Education and within reach of Kasuga Taisha and Shin-Yakushiji. The cafe was founded decades ago by a Japanese proprietor, Setsuo Sakamoto, who built its reputation on a distinctive curry. After his passing, his French wife, Miriam — for whom the shop is named — has continued to run it, keeping its character intact inside a hand-renovated old wooden house. · A deliberately tranquil room with vintage furnishings and pendant lamps and no background music, made for slow, unhurried meals. · The signature is a fragrant Indian-style beef curry: chunks of beef brisket simmered with eight spices for about three hours and then rested a full day, served over rice with raisins and a side of plain yogurt that diners can stir in to soften the heat. A chicken stew is also offered. Miriam bakes homemade Western-style cakes and pastries daily — including gateau chocolat — which draw their own devoted regulars, with seasonal touches like ratatouille in summer.
places.gfd: No gluten-free offerings or accommodations are documented. places.chef: owner, yakuzen (medicinal-herb) coordinator · 8nosu is a small spice-curry-and-honey shop tucked into a traditional wooden townhouse in Nara's Naramachi district, a short walk south of Sarusawa Pond and Kofuku-ji Temple. It is run by a certified yakuzen (medicinal-herb cooking) coordinator who built the menu around the idea of food as everyday wellness. · Built on the motto 食べて元気になる - eat and become well - applying medicinal-herb principles so a casual curry lunch doubles as nourishment. · Stone-bowl soup curry built from about 20 spices and seasonal medicinal-herb vegetables. Diners choose a base (vegetable-only, soft chicken, or slow-braised pork), a soup style (original, coconut, or shrimp), and a spice level. places.gfd: No gluten-free claim is published. A celiac diner would need to ask directly and should not assume it is safe.

places.chef: owner-maker · Nara, Japan · Shika san chocolat opened in late 2023 as a one-product specialty stand inside the Yume CUBE, the entrepreneur-support corner of Nara's historic Mochiidono Center-gai shopping arcade. Its owner runs it as a second venture alongside Milleturu, a women's tailoring atelier based in nearby Yamato-Koriyama, and spent more than a decade perfecting a single idea: a gateau au chocolat unlike any other. · The maker set out to create 'a new standard no one has tasted before,' framing the chocolate-to-sansho transition as a journey ending in Nara, the terminus of the Silk Road. The flourless approach is central to the recipe rather than an afterthought. · A sansho (Japanese mountain pepper) gateau au chocolat — a rich-but-clean-finishing, fluffy-yet-moist chocolate cake in which the chocolate slowly gives way to bright Japanese-pepper notes, using stone-ground 'budo-sansho' from the Kii Peninsula. It is made entirely without wheat flour, rice flour or baking powder. Sold by the cut, half, and whole cake; a plain version without sansho is also offered for those who prefer it.

places.chef: owner, kakigori chef · Nara, Japan · Gentry first opened in April 1984 as an old-school jazz bar in central Nara, spinning jazz on vinyl and hosting occasional live performances. Over four decades it became beloved less for its records than for an unlikely signature: an elaborate flambeed shaved ice. After closing its long-time home in the Shimomikado shopping street in April 2024 to the sadness of many regulars, it returned in late October 2025 a few steps from Kintetsu Nara Station, now billed as Kakigori & Whisky Gentry, still built around its Swan ice shaver and jazz-bar mood. · The house specialty is yaki-gori, baked shaved ice: layers of azuki beans, lemon jelly and condensed milk under a matcha meringue that the owner blowtorches to a caramelized crust, then douses with flambeed Cointreau so the mountain of ice briefly catches fire, a nod to Nara's Wakakusa-yama grass-burning festival. Seasonal creations rotate through flavors such as pistachio and white chocolate, pumpkin, strawberry, and custard brulee. By night it pours whisky, wine and cocktails.
places.gfd: No gluten-free offering. The signature shaved ice is layered with components such as lemon jelly, azuki red beans, condensed milk and matcha meringue, with no documented gluten-free menu or allergen handling. Toppings and accompanying sweets are not verified as wheat-free, and there is no information about cross-contamination control. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan. places.chef: 廣岡夏主 (Hirooka Natsushi, who goes by the nickname "Nassh") · owner, chef · The owner ran a creative izakaya near JR Nara Station for roughly six years before relocating in January 2024 to a quietly renovated machiya (traditional townhouse) in the Naramachi district, near the Imanishi Seibei brewery (maker of Harushika sake). Other signatures pair Nara produce with European technique, such as cold peach pasta with Yamato beef prosciutto, young-corn fritters with white-miso aioli, and a 'wa-hijo' (Japanese-style ajillo) of firefly squid and rape blossoms.

places.chef: Shinsuke Yamamoto · owner, proprietor · Nara, Japan · The shop opened in April 2012 in a white-walled traditional townhouse just off the Mochiidono arcade, on a site that had previously been the sake shop Sakagura Sasaya. It occupies a historic merchant quarter near Todai-ji, Kofuku-ji and Gangoji. The proprietor, Shinsuke Yamamoto, is a former researcher and director at Nara's prefectural industrial technology center with a background in fermentation chemistry — expertise he drew on, including work connected to reviving the ancient monk-brewed Bodaisen sake. · Celebrates Nara's claim as a birthplace of clear refined sake, giving visitors an approachable, low-commitment way to explore the prefecture's breweries (such as Harushika and Hatsugasumi) and discover a favorite with staff guidance. · Paid by-the-glass tasting of around 120 regional sake from roughly 30 breweries across Nara Prefecture, poured in small 50cc glasses from about 150 yen, with comparison sets (pure-rice, ginjo, dry) and the option to buy a bottle of anything you like. Snacks lean on Nara's food heritage — hishio (a revived ancient koji seasoning), sake-lees cream cheese and Nara pickles.
places.gfd: This is a sake tasting bar, not a kitchen. Sake (junmai/ginjo) is brewed from rice, water and koji and is generally gluten-free, so the core offering of by-the-glass tastings is broadly suitable. However, this is not a celiac-focused venue and there is no published allergen handling. Accompanying small plates include items such as hishio (a koji-based fermented seasoning), aged sake-lees cream cheese and Nara pickles (narazuke) — narazuke and some seasonings are cured in sake lees / may involve…
places.vgd: Drinks-focused venue. Most sake is vegan, though sake filtration/processing is not disclosed here. Food is limited to a few snacks: Nara pickles (narazuke) and koji-based hishio are plant-based, but the aged sake-lees cream cheese is dairy. There is no dedicated vegan menu — vegans can taste sake and choose pickle-type snacks but should ask about each item.
places.hours: 11:00–20:00, closed Thursdays (open if Thursday falls on a national holiday); occasional temporary closures announced on the official site.

places.chef: owner, chef · Nara, Japan · A small, hidden-gem Chinese restaurant tucked down a narrow alley off the Higashimuki shopping street, a few minutes' walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. It is run almost single-handedly by its owner-chef, who has relocated the shop at least once over the years. · The chef prizes freshness over speed, cutting vegetables to order and avoiding chemical seasonings, building a 'light, gentle and colorful' style of Chinese cooking that leans on Nara-grown ingredients — Yamato pork, Yamato beef, Yamato vegetables and local tofu — to create a distinctly Nara take on Chinese food. · Charcoal-grilled gyoza filled with Yamato pork and cabbage (softened with added tofu) and made without garlic; and the house mapo tofu, made with locally grown soybean tofu and fragrant Japanese pepper for a savory, brightly numbing heat. Vinegar chicken and a seafood-and-vegetable chanpon are also local favorites.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. This is a Chinese kitchen built around gyoza (wheat wrappers), wheat-based soy sauce, and likely flour-thickened/wok dishes; there is no dedicated gluten-free handling and cross-contact is unavoidable. Not safe for celiac diners.
places.vgd: Not a vegan destination. The kitchen centers on Yamato pork, Yamato beef and seafood; signature dishes (gyoza, mapo tofu, vinegar chicken) are meat/fish-based. Even the locally made tofu dishes are cooked in meat- or fish-derived sauces. The gyoza being garlic-free is a flavor choice, not a vegan one. Vegans would need to ask, and options would be very limited at best.

places.chef: ramen shop, tsukemen specialist · Nara (Higashimuki arcade, near Kintetsu Nara Station) · A chicken-paitan ramen and tsukemen shop tucked into the Higashimuki covered arcade, a two-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. It is run as part of a small local restaurant group (the Hiten group, which also operates the nearby Chinese kitchen Hiten), and the Nara branch is descended from an earlier ramen shop on the site once known as 'Nara Ramen Aoniyoshi,' rebranded around the end of 2011. · An emphasis on a long-simmered, made-from-scratch chicken paitan base and self-made noodles, paired with local Nara rice. · The kitchen builds everything on a milky tori paitan broth simmered for hours from chicken bones, whole chicken, vegetables and kombu. The flagship is the chicken-paitan tsukemen, with house-made medium-thick noodles from domestic whole-grain (mineral-rich whole-wheat) flour and Nara-grown rice. Tourist-friendly specials round out the menu, including the lavish Daibutsu (Great Buddha) ramen topped with shrimp tempura, fried mochi, char siu and soft-boiled egg, and the lighter Asuka soy-milk paitan ramen.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free in any meaningful way. The core menu is wheat ramen and tsukemen — the shop makes its own noodles from domestic wheat flour (and mineral-rich whole-grain wheat flour for the tsukemen), serves gyoza (wheat wrappers), and uses chicken/vegetable/kombu broth typically finished with standard seasonings. No celiac-safe options and no dedicated handling reported.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans. places.chef: 西 奈槻 (Nishi Natsuki) & 奥野 亮太郎 (Okuno Ryotaro) · founder, owner, cook · Nara, Japan; founded by Kinki University students · Two friends and Kinki University students (Faculty of Agriculture, Department of Aquaculture) started the shop during the 2020 pandemic. Nishi, a former aspiring drummer who felt adrift after giving up that dream, spent the COVID lockdown visiting local Nara business owners to explore his future. On his third visit, the owner of a Naramachi halal ramen shop offered to hand over the space; Nishi immediately called Okuno, a friend known for his cooking and obsession with mapo tofu, who agreed on the spot. They first opened as 'jinniyah / 奈KAMA' in October 2020, then rebranded to 'すするか、すすらんか。' on June 6, 2021. · The name means roughly 'Shall we slurp, or shan't we?' — a play on the founder's mantra '結局やるか、やらんかやで' ('In the end it comes down to whether you do it or not'). They see the shop as more than a restaurant: a way to show young people in Japan that they have choices ('日本の若者に選択肢を'), running initiatives like inviting young people to submit recipes and hosting one-day managers to spark conversations about life paths. · Their flagship is the mapo tofu ramen cal…
places.gfd: This is a ramen shop whose entire concept is a wheat-noodle dish. The signature mapo tofu ramen uses standard medium-thick wheat noodles, and the mapo sauce relies on doubanjiang and fermented soybeans (typically wheat-containing) plus a chicken-bone broth. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no allergen handling information. Not suitable for celiacs or anyone needing strict gluten avoidance.

places.chef: owner · Opened in autumn 2015 alongside the renovated National Treasure Hall (Kokuhoden) of Kasuga Taisha, this cafe and shop sits on the first floor of the museum building within the shrine's sacred grounds in Nara Park. · The space is built to carry the feeling of Kasuga's primeval forest indoors: its counter is fashioned from a Kasuga cedar that grew on the mountain and was felled by a lightning strike in the Showa era, and other wooden fittings are made from nagi, a tree designated a natural monument. It was founded by the Murakami family to be a neighborhood bread shop rooted in their home city of Nara. · To make gentle, everyday bread that children and elderly customers alike can enjoy, kept at approachable prices and convenient hours, using domestic wheat and local Nara ingredients such as Yamato tea and Nara-grown rice so the bakery stays tied to its hometown. · The signature 'Hibi no Shokupan' (daily milk-style loaf) made from a proprietary blend of domestic wheat and Nara rice, with a soft, chewy crumb that is faintly sweet eaten plain and crisp-edged when toasted. places.hood: Kitamachi (Hōren-chō) / Kintetsu Nara Stn
places.notes: SAHHA is a Tunisian and North African restaurant tucked inside a renovated traditional Japanese house (kominka) in the Kitamachi district of Nara, near Nara Women's University. It opened in August 2021 and is one of very few places in Nara — and rare even nationwide in Japan — se
places.chef: Madani Imed · owner, chef · Tunisia · SAHHA is a Tunisian and North African restaurant tucked inside a renovated traditional Japanese house (kominka) in the Kitamachi district of Nara, on a corner northwest of Nara Women's University. It opened in August 2021 and is one of very few places in Nara — and rare even nationwide in Japan — serving authentic Tunisian home cooking. The owner, Madani Imed, from Tunisia, runs the place together with his Japanese partner, with his mother's Tataouine-style home cooking at the heart of the kitchen. · Every dish on the menu is halal, so Muslim travelers can eat freely, and the kitchen leans heavily on fresh vegetables — cabbage, chickpeas, dates, radish, zucchini, onion and carrot — giving vegetarians and vegans some honest options too. · Couscous is the signature: the traditional couscous (around ¥1,400) is built on the world's smallest pasta soaking up a tomato-based broth simmered with root vegetables and lamb, finished with a hint of raisin sweetness. Other beloved dishes include kebsa (an Arab-style spiced long-grain rice biryani with lamb or chicken, described as milder than its Indian counterpart), shakshuka (a Tunisian tomato-and-vegeta…
places.gfd: No dedicated gluten-free program. The signature dish is couscous, which is wheat-based semolina pasta and unsafe for celiacs. However, some naturally gluten-free items exist: falafel (chickpea), shakshuka (a tomato/vegetable stew), and rice-based kebsa/biryani. Cross-contamination is not addressed in any source, and harissa/spice blends and sauces have unverified ingredients. A gluten-free diner would need to ask the owner directly about each dish.
places.vgd: The restaurant explicitly offers some vegan-appropriate and vegetarian dishes. Documented plant-based options include falafel (chickpea, ~¥1,300) and shakshuka (Tunisian vegetable/tomato stew, ~¥1,200), and the kitchen emphasizes fresh vegetables (cabbage, chickpeas, dates, radish, zucchini, onion, carrot). It is not a fully vegan restaurant — couscous and kebsa dishes are prepared with lamb or c…

places.chef: owner · Nara (Naramachi district) · A specialty tofu-sweets café in the historic Naramachi neighborhood (Tsurufukuin-cho), about a 10-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station and minutes from Sarusawa Pond. The Naramachi location opened in early 2023 (pre-opening on weekends in late January, with the grand opening in February 2023), joining the brand's popular sibling shops in Osaka's Nakazakicho and Kobe's Motomachi. · The café centers on 'guilt-free,' health-conscious sweets made with tofu that are described as creamy and indulgent without tasting of tofu. · Handmade tofu tiramisu served in a small wooden box, offered in flavors such as cocoa, matcha, hojicha, black sesame, mango, and a seasonal fresh-strawberry version ('Ichigo kaoru tofu tiramisu'). places.n: うな菊 奈良本店 (Unakiku Nara Honten)
places.hood: Takabatake / in front of Kasuga Taisha first torii gate, wit
places.notes: Unakiku is a dedicated eel restaurant born from Kikusuiro, a celebrated ryotei founded in 1891 (Meiji 24) and now a registered tangible cultural property, set directly in front of the first torii gate of Kasuga Taisha shrine. For more than 130 years the house has welcomed disting
places.chef: unagi specialist, historic ryotei (Kikusuiro) · Nara, Japan · Unakiku is a dedicated eel restaurant born from Kikusuiro, a celebrated ryotei founded in 1891 (Meiji 24) and now a registered tangible cultural property, set directly in front of the first torii gate of Kasuga Taisha shrine. For more than 130 years the house has welcomed distinguished guests, and Unakiku carries that hospitality into a focused eel specialty. · The restaurant frames eating eel as part of a pilgrimage ritual, building on the local custom of enjoying unagi after visiting Kasuga Taisha, and aims to connect people through eel cuisine. · Edo-style unagi: live eels are filleted to order, white-grilled, thoroughly steamed, then charcoal-grilled with the house tare. Signature dishes include the classic unagi-don and the ainose-don, which pairs plain white-grilled eel (shirayaki) with tare-glazed eel in one bowl. The tare blends pure additive-free Tenno Shoyu soy sauce (brewed with Fuji spring water) and traditional hon-mirin, and the rice is exclusively Niigata Uonuma Koshihikari grown for the restaurant by a partner farmer.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The signature unagi is grilled and finished with a tare made from wheat-based soy sauce (Tenno Shoyu) and mirin, so the core dish contains gluten. No dedicated gluten-free menu, preparation, or accommodation is documented. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. This is a dedicated freshwater-eel (unagi) specialist; the entire menu centers on grilled live eel. No plant-based dishes are documented.

places.n: オーセンティックテーブル タバーン (Authentic Table Tavern)
places.hood: 下三条町 (Shimosanjo-cho), on Sanjo-dori near Kintetsu Nara & JR
places.notes: A casual French dining room set on Sanjo-dori, the historic street running between Nara Station and Kasuga Taisha Shrine, in a warm interior of natural-wood tones meant for relaxed special occasions.
places.chef: sommelier on staff · A casual French dining room set on Sanjo-dori, the historic street running between Nara Station and Kasuga Taisha Shrine, in a warm interior of natural-wood tones meant for relaxed special occasions. · The kitchen aims to honor the natural flavor of its ingredients, sourcing seasonal Yamato vegetables and premium produce and using special sauces and spices only as refined accents rather than to mask the food. · Charcoal-grilled cooking is the heart of the kitchen, built around carefully chosen ingredients from Nara and Hokkaido. Signature plates include charcoal-grilled steak and vegetables, fresh charcoal-grilled fish, a house specialty soup curry, and homemade ham made from Yamato pork (served with onion sauce), all paired with an extensive sommelier-curated wine list.
places.gfd: No gluten-free program is documented. This is a casual French/yoshoku restaurant whose menu includes sauces, homemade ham, soup curry and charcoal-grilled dishes; flour-based sauces and wheat are common in this cuisine, so it is not celiac-safe without direct confirmation. A celiac diner must ask the kitchen about every dish.
places.vgd: No vegan menu is documented. The kitchen does source seasonal Yamato vegetables from Nara and grills vegetables such as broccoli, but the menu centers on charcoal-grilled meats, fresh fish, homemade Yamato-pork ham and dairy-based French preparations. There may be vegetable side dishes, but no confirmed plant-only mains; a vegan diner should call ahead and ask.

places.chef: owner-bakers (husband and wife) · Nara, Japan · BAKERY GEN is a small neighborhood bakery run by a husband-and-wife team in the Sakyo residential district of northern Nara, set among the Heijo-Sakyo (Takanohara) housing estates. The couple bake roughly 40 kinds of bread by hand each day and pride themselves on being close to their customers, often turning conversations at the counter into new products on the shelves. · They describe themselves as a bakery that stays close to the community, adjusting the blend of several wheat flours to suit each bread and recipe, drawing on years of accumulated technique, and developing new breads from customer feedback. · Their best-known item is the cream pan, filled with rich hand-strained custard cream made fresh to pair with their dough. Other favorites include a salted potato focaccia, an egg-free fluffy milk bread using quality fresh cream, and a buttery kouign-amann.
places.gfd: This is a conventional wheat-flour bakery; the owners blend several types of wheat flour for their breads, and signature items (cream pan, milk bread, focaccia, kouign-amann) are all wheat-based. There is no gluten-free offering and no measures against cross-contamination documented. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-avoidant diners.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] The chef trained at prestigious Tokyo hotels and restaurants before opening this small Italian cafe in 2017 in Takabatake-cho, his wife's hometown, in a quiet corner of central Nara near the Nara Hotel.
places.chef: chef-owner · Tokyo fine-dining background; settled in Nara. · The chef trained at prestigious Tokyo hotels and restaurants before opening this small Italian cafe in 2017 in Takabatake-cho, his wife's hometown, in a quiet corner of central Nara near the Nara Hotel. · He frames the shaved ice in light of Nara's long history of worshipping the guardian deity of ice since the Heijo-kyo era, and treats kakigori as a dish rather than a sweet — building flavors with techniques borrowed from Western cooking. He offers it only irregularly, woven into the restaurant's schedule (announced via Instagram), valuing quality over convenience. · Creative Italian cooking using local Nara ingredients, plus a celebrated summer shaved ice. The signature is a Garden Plum Soda kakigori made from syrup pressed from the large plum tree growing on the property, layered with umeboshi paste for a sweet-tart-salty profile and a fizzing carbonated jelly at the bottom. His fine-dining background also produces savory, Italian-style kakigori such as a white-tomato version finished with basil sauce and cultured (sour) cream.
places.gfd: This is an Italian kitchen built around pasta and Western dishes, so wheat is central and there is no indication of gluten-free accommodation; not suitable for celiacs. The kakigori may be naturally wheat-light but no gluten-free handling is documented.
places.vgd: No vegan menu is documented. It is a creative Italian restaurant likely using meat, fish, dairy and eggs, and the signature kakigori use syrups, umeboshi paste and a tomato-and-sour-cream version that is not vegan. A vegan diner would need to ask directly about any plant-based options.

places.chef: 奥谷美樹 (Okutani Miki) · owner, shaved ice maker · The owner left a career as a securities trader to pursue a long-held passion for kakigori, spending roughly a year of preparation before opening the shop in 2019 rather than launching before the quality met their standards. · Relentless quality control, with the owner describing themselves as the harshest critic of their own shaved ice; the ice is shaved for a fluffy texture and served in vessels chosen to slow melting. · House-made shaved ice with from-scratch syrups: a salted coconut-pineapple bowl finished with Nara konpeito candy from a long-established Nara confectioner founded in the Ansei era (mid-1800s), a 'MAX Ginger / 本気の生姜' bowl built for intense ginger umami, and a seasonal 'ミラコロいちご' using Nara's premium Koto-ka (古都華) strawberries with crème d'ange.

places.chef: izakaya, creative Nara cuisine, local sake · Nara, Japan · Itadakiya sits in Shimo-Sanjo-cho on Sanjo-dori, the historic approach toward Kasuga Taisha that has served pilgrims into Nara for centuries, a few minutes' walk from Kintetsu and JR Nara stations. It is run by the Nara restaurant company Ing (株式会社イング), under the easygoing concept of a 'teishoku eatery where you can also drink' — comfortable enough for a quiet dinner or a group banquet. · Showcasing Nara's terroir — the kitchen selects vegetables daily and leans on nationally known Yamato heirloom varieties alongside local meats and sake, so a meal doubles as a tour of regional produce. · Creative 'Nara-meshi' cooking that puts local Yamato ingredients front and center: Yamato chicken and Yamato pork grilled as skewers over the robata, Yamato heirloom vegetables, and seasonal Nara produce chosen fresh each day. A signature is a green-tea-broth shabu hot pot with Yamato pork, paired with sake brought in from Nara-area breweries.
places.gfd: No gluten-free program or labeling found on any page. This is a soy-sauce, sake, and tempura-heavy izakaya (fried items, grilled skewers with tare, simmered dishes), so wheat exposure is pervasive and it is not suitable for celiacs. No allergy or gluten information is published.
places.vgd: A meat-and-fish izakaya centered on Yamato beef, pork, and chicken. It does feature Yamato heirloom vegetables and vegetable tempura, but no dedicated vegan menu exists and dashi/soy seasonings make most dishes non-vegan. A flexible vegan might find a few plain vegetable plates but should ask in advance; no vegan info is published.

places.chef: Ohana-san · owner, chef, sole operator · Wajima, Ishikawa Prefecture · Originally from Wajima in Ishikawa Prefecture, the owner known as Ohana-san worked as a sales representative in Osaka before moving to Nara in 2013 out of deep affection for the city. places.notes: [GF] Michelin-listed, Tabelog-100 jūwari soba shop where both the seiro and inaka soba are 100% buckwheat with no wheat binder, boiled to order. The noodle is celiac-plausible but the soy-based tsuyu and shared boiling water are the risk — go at lunch, ask for tamari tsuyu and dedicated water, and skip any tempura. places.chef: Hiroyuki Shimazaki (島﨑宏之) · owner, soba chef · Japan · Gen is run by owner-chef Hiroyuki Shimazaki in a quiet house in Naramachi's Fukuchiin-cho. Before soba, Shimazaki worked as a craftsman shaving reeds for woodwind instruments, precision work measured at the micron level, and he carries that exactness into milling and cutting. He stone-grinds only the day's portion of buckwheat each morning and cuts the jūwari noodles ultra-thin so they cook quickly without a binder. The shop appears repeatedly in the Michelin guide and on Tabelog's soba-100 list. · Freshly self-milled buckwheat, no tsunagi (wheat binder), noodles cut thin and boiled by the portion for peak aroma. · Jūwari seiro and inaka (hull-in) soba; mizu-soba with ume

places.notes: [GF] — One of very few places in Japan where a celiac can eat authentic Neapolitan pizza: GF dough/pasta/dessert are made in an isolated wheat-free lab and served on a marked plate, and the owner is a GF-category world champion. The catch is that this is a full wheat pizzeria — flour is airborne and the wood oven bakes regular dough — so this is ASK, not celiac-safe by default. Tell them clearly you have celiac disease (セリアック病) and ask them to confirm the GF pizza's baking and plating are kept separate from the wheat line before you order.
places.chef: Nakanishi (中西) · owner, pizzaiolo · Nara, Japan · Owner-pizzaiolo Nakanishi trained in Naples (under gluten-free pioneer Domenico Scola) and opened Pizzeria ICARO in Nara's Nijō-ōji Minami district (near Suzakumon of the Heijō Palace site) in May 2017. He built the shop around a wood-fired oven for traditional Neapolitan pizza but added a dedicated, isolated gluten-free lab and a separate GF oven so that people with celiac disease, gluten intolerance and allergies could enjoy real pizza and pasta. The venue explicitly frames its gluten-free work as being for medical need rather than as a diet trend. · 「小麦グルテンを摂取することで様々な不調をもたらすセリアック病やグルテン不耐症、アレルギーの方に安心安全にピッツァやパスタを提供する」 — to let those who cannot eat wheat gluten enjoy authentic pizza and pasta, not as a fad. · Authentic Neapolitan wood-fired pizza, with a gluten-free crust/pasta/dessert line
